Age-old handwritten documents stored in national libraries and archives suffer from
degradation due to time, resulting in the distortion of written text. Restoration of
these documents for better readability is crucial, primarily to improve text
legibility. Current methods mainly focus on enhancing the visual appearance but
don't guarantee better readability. In contrast, this study introduces a novel
multi-task adversarial network (MTAN) called the Text Enhancement Network (TEN),
designed to boost the readability of degraded documents. By leveraging a
bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) structure for text feature
extraction, a generative adversarial model for image enhancement, and a CNN
classification head for page classification, TEN achieves remarkable results on
popular datasets, outperforming existing methods.

The extraction of information from official documents is a crucial process that cannot be fully automated due to complex layout issues and the necessity to adapt to various document types. This study presents an Indonesian ID card extractor that employs a combination of Optical Character Recognition and Natural Language Processing to accurately extract and process information from Indonesian ID cards. The proposed method leverages a layout analysis algorithm to fine-tune the OCR results, thereby enhancing their precision and facilitating further processing of the extracted data.

In vehicular communication systems, the reliability of channel assessment is the key to successful data transfer. However, existing methods used in IEEE 802.11p networks, such as single-value assessment, are insufficient for real-time video transmission. Since channel conditions can remain stable for a few milliseconds, considering short time windows may not fully utilize this stability. Most deep learning-based approaches for channel assessment focus on real-time predictions and do not leverage this stability. This paper introduces a new deep learning-based method that employs temporal averaging of LSTM-based models to exploit this stability in IEEE 802.11p networks. The proposed approach is evaluated using both emulated and actual channel impairment scenarios, and the results show its superiority over existing methods.

The remarkable achievements of Deep Learning technologies, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), have allowed for the accurate replication of complex datasets in a wide array of fields. GANs have been successfully used in data enhancement and colorization applications. In the context of Astronomy, these techniques hold significant potential for mitigating issues arising from noisy or partially exposed CCD images. This thesis delves into the use of GANs for colorization and image enhancement purposes. The colorization approach, for instance, involves generating new, pseudo-color images from narrowband fake points, producing more lifelike representations of Celestial objects. The focus on brown dwarfs and extremely low-mass stars enables the evaluation of their spectral classification through weak lensing analysis or the identification of these objects within the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS). Moreover, a method is proposed to convert narrowband images into physical flux distributions, opening up possibilities for the simulation of mock observations. The application of PCA for dimensionality reduction in spectral data is explored as a potential means of whitening this data, thereby facilitating the generation of fake spectra that accurately resemble observed spectral patterns. This approach can provide supplementary information for the analysis of mock spectra, including noise profiles and redshifts. The integration of a teacher-forcing strategy during training is shown to yield improved results in the spectrum generation task.

Despite the impressive performance of deep neural networks (DNNs), their complex training process, specifically the backpropagation phase with numerous derivatives, has hindered broader adoption. A novel approach seeks to bypass this limitation by reframing the DNN as a continuous function that can be directly input and output, thus eliminating the need for backpropagation. Building upon the Universal Approximation Theorem, this method claims that any continuous function can be expressed as a sum of weighted and locally scaled unit activations. However, this claim is challenged by the infinite dimensionality of unit activations, which cannot be applied practically. Therefore, this problem is reformulated as an infinite dimensional linear regression problem with restricted parameters. Utilizing the Unconstrained Optimization Framework, orthogonality constraints are imposed on the weights as a way to alleviate the 'curse of dimensionality'. Simulation results demonstrate that a 5-layer DNN with orthogonal weights can perform universal function approximation with high accuracy, often surpassing state-of-the-art methods.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECR) serves as a vital representative body, expressing the views and interests of young researchers working in experimental particle physics within ECFA. Formed in January 2021, the committee comprises 30 young researchers from 29 laboratories across Europe and Israel, covering a broad range of research domains. Throughout its initial term, the ECR committee engaged in various activities, including multiple online meetings, focus group discussions on key topics such as diversity, equity, and inclusion, and community building. This report outlines the committee's purpose, composition, and accomplishments during its first term of office.

Recent advancements in planar metasurfaces have contributed significantly to enhancing our understanding of the steering of electromagnetic waves at microwave frequencies. However, the current state-of-the-art technology for optical frequencies still heavily relies on bulk nonlinear crystals or microresonators. To bridge this gap, we propose and demonstrate a novel approach using a dual metasurface to control ripples in optical wave steering. By integrating two metasurfaces, each comprising a gold patch on a gold screen, we successfully devise various phase ripples and achieve significant control over optical wave propagation. Notably, our findings reveal that the inherent gold platform itself functions as a microsurfaces-based ripples steering element, offering a groundbreaking possibility for incorporating ripples steering capabilities directly into optical systems.

This paper addresses the need for adaptive Cognition-Aware Architectures that enable collaborative learning between humans and robots across a wide range of applications and domains. As distributed AI systems, spanning from the edge to the cloud, necessitate more efficient and scalable design, such as cognitive architectures for multi-agent learning. We propose a multi-level architecture that facilitates large-scale multi-agent collaboration through cloud-based cognition, and implement this using a distributed Kubernetes system as an underlying infrastructure. The implementation demonstrates the feasibility of this approach through a basic human-robot collaboration task, and our future plans involve enhancing the architecture for more complex applications and evaluating its performance under different conditions.

A widely used measure of variability in data is the mean absolute deviation (MAD) around the median. This measure is preferred due to its simplicity and robustness over measures like the standard deviation. The sample version of MAD is biased by itself in asymptotic terms and needs to be corrected for accurate estimates. The purpose of this paper is to discuss two specific bias-correlated estimators of the population MAD proposed in the study and compare them with the existing estimators in terms of the convergence rate and consistency. The study also evaluates the performance of these estimators through simulations and applies them to analyze variability in remote working patterns across different fields.

The accuracy of relation extraction can be significantly improved by utilizing knowledge graph link prediction, according to recent research. Nonetheless, applying this technique to real-world datasets remains complicated due to the differing scales of relation extraction and link prediction tasks. Most existing models can handle either task but face challenges with the other. To overcome these limitations, a new hybrid model called HyKE has been created, combining keystone network technology to effectively tackle datasets of varying sizes. By doing so, HyKE enables the shared representations of relation extraction and link prediction tasks to be exploited, thus enhancing the overall performance and scalability.

In this study, we examine the changes in the binding energy and dissociation temperature of quarkonia in a hot, complex QCD medium with momentum asymmetry in a N-dimensional space to explore the impact of finite baryonic chemical potential. To achieve this, we calculate the Debye mass using quasi-particle theory and incorporate finite baryonic potential into the HARTREE-Fock-QMT potential model. The results show that as momentum asymmetry increases, the binding energy of quarkonia decreases, leading to a drop in dissociation temperatures. Additionally, we find that at finite baryonic potential, the characteristics of quarkonia are significantly affected, resulting in lowered binding energy and dissociation temperatures compared to situations without momentum asymmetry or baryonic potential.

We investigated the magnetic arrangements in Tb3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction measurements, discovering that this material exhibits two distinct types of magnetic ordering. In regions containing chains of Ru ions, a uniform 1/2 magnetic ordering occurs within these chains. However, this material exhibits an unconventional magnetic behavior confined to the Tb3+ ions surrounding the chains, resulting in an unusual magnetic state. Through detailed data analysis, we found that Tb3RuO7 exhibits long-range magnetic order with a temperature transition at 1.34 K, transitioning into a disordered state with increased entropy above this temperature threshold.

The primary goal of our artwork and accompanying technical section is to demonstrate how Modulated Periodic Activations can effectively generate detailed, high-resolution images of brain areas, akin to historical anatomical paintings. Our method employs a network design that alternates between reflection and convolution, resulting in a more realistic and detailed representation of brain regions. The Modulated Periodic Activations method offers an attractive alternative to traditional activation functions, particularly for visual applications. Our technical section provides a detailed description of the MPA structure, its parameters, and the training objectives that enable the generation of visually appealing and informative brain area depictions.

Machine learning models can make predictions on data with varying covariate profiles, but this capability is crucial for addressing shifts in covariate distribution in real-world scenarios. We've developed a novel prediction technique utilizing causal models to account for such shifts, drawing from the theory of semi-generative models. By combining invariance principles and representation learning, semi-generative models balance representation and prediction tasks. We've adapted this framework to deal with covariate shifts, leveraging effective techniques like importance weighting and maximum likelihood estimation for practical use. Our approach is demonstrated to work effectively on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks. This exploration is linked to the broader concept of solving equilibrium problems within complex systems, as well as the study of geometric statistical mechanics, which draws on connections to the replica method and cavity approach. Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop new insights into the structure and function of deep learning models, ultimately enabling the development of innovative algorithms for solving learning problems.

In algebraic geometry, we explore the underlying lattices of CM modules attached to quadratic forms arising from period spaces of certain modular forms. Period spaces associated with kernel lattices of cusp forms for $\mathrm{GL}_2$ can be represented as modular varieties, and our focus lies in lattices defined over number fields that arise in these periods. These CM modules provide substantial insight into the structure of these periods. We establish the fundamental building blocks of these lattices as modules over their corresponding number fields and identify the primary components as products of lattice modifications and ring extensions. Furthermore, we determine the minimal lattices within these CM modules, and in cases where the lattice is maximal, we explicitly compute the lattice basis. Our work specifically investigates lattices related to holomorphic modular forms, elliptic modular forms, and certain weight-$k$ modular forms for $\mathrm{SL}_2$ or $\mathrm{GL}_2$, and we presents accompanying computer programs to facilitate lattice construction and analysis.

Deep neural network jet classifiers, used to identify particles created from the decay of high-energy particles called quarks and gluons, have achieved remarkable accuracy in simulated data and are becoming increasingly essential in high-energy physics research. However, the complex networks make it difficult to grasp the classification process. To address this issue, we use the LRP (LayerWise Relevance Propagation) method to analyze and interpret the decision-making process of these classifiers. By replacing key images, we uncover crucial visual cues essential for classification, and demonstrate that the LRP can be applied even to sophisticated networks with numerous layers, using the example of the ResNet. Additionally, we introduce 'expert variables' which are simplified networks that mimic the behavior of the complex network, allowing us to evaluate whether the network has overfit or accurately represents the input data. This tool is then utilized on the top layer of the network to break down classification results into distinct contributions.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

We categorize the non-irreducible representations of double coverings for both gray and ordinary double strata groups within two-dimensional space. Our analysis considers site symmetry as a factor and achieves a comprehensive listing of compatible symmetry sets, along with the associated multiplication tables for gray strata groups, an area of study previously unexplored until now. By leveraging the connection between band topology and group representation, we derive the numerical count for band insulators, metals, and semimetals based on the established double coverings' irreducible representations.

Momentum operators with continuous spectrum are explored in relation to Killing vectors representing geodesic curves on a manifold. It is demonstrated that for compact manifolds, the momentum operators are skew-Hermitian, which has significant implications for the behavior of free fields and their compliance with the Einstein causality principle. Additionally, the study establishes the completeness of orthogonal basis sets for the tensor fields resulting from the action of finite-dimensional Lie algebras on the manifold.

A major limitation of using neural networks to simulate quantum systems has been the significant sign error found in the results, particularly in the study of Hubbert models. This sign error made the computation unreliable and quickly caused the loss to skyrocket during training. We discovered that the cause of this sign error was linked to the way the non-linear activation function behaved. This issue could be avoided by modifying the activation function to handle complex numbers instead of just real numbers. By doing so, the sign error was largely eliminated, and the computation became much more precise. Furthermore, the model's performance was enhanced as it no longer experienced the dramatic boost in loss during training.

In composite Higgs theories, where a flavor symmetry breaks spontaneously in a coset space, flavor and a flavor-breaking scale can be distinct, allowing for a flavon-Higgs mixing that significantly impacts the flavor physics consequences. This is in stark contrast to the standard, unscaled flavor symmetry scenario. We've explored the flavon-Higgs mixing effects on flavor-changing neutral currents and precision electroweak experiments, determining the feasible parameter regions based on current constraints. Notably, our findings indicate that a flavor-physics-driven bound on the CP-odd Higgs coupling to gluons and a LHC-based bound on the CP-odd Higgs coupling to gluons are the most stringent constraints on the flavon-Higgs mixing in this theory. This has also led us to conduct an additional analysis within an example case, where we've examined flavor physics consequences in a simple model featuring a $SU(4)/SU(3)\times U(1)$ coset space and including a scalar sector with two flavon-Higgs doublets.

The use of Virtual-Physical Interaction enables users to manipulate digital objects within VR by using real-world objects, which can stimulate vision and touch. This fusion of real and digital objects potentially triggers perceptual distortions that may have significant psychological and physical effects on users. This study investigates these distortions and their impacts, revealing the risks associated with VR technology. The findings of this research can contribute to the design of safe and intuitive interfaces for VPIN systems, thus minimizing user distress and safeguarding their physical well-being.

To assess various approaches to adding new languages to a multilingual model, we conduct our study using the BigScience large-scale pre-trained multilingual transformer model. This model supports 13 different languages and a combined total of 7.5 billion words from Wikipedia and WebData datasets. We focus our study on two "exotic" languages – Khmer and Mongolian – and by extending the model to process these languages, we successfully achieve accurate zero-shot translation results for both languages. We then test several training schedules on languages that are closely related to the original 13 but have never been seen during training. Our experiments reveal that the model's performance in these languages heavily relies on the available parallel data and that the gradient-based training schedules tend to yield superior results compared to batch-based approaches. We also analyze the model's embeddings to gain insight into its performance and find that the model's performance in these languages heavily relies on the available parallel data and that the model is capable of learning distinct language characteristics.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unseen details of binary systems, particularly their mass distribution and separation spacing. Our numerical simulations replicate the binary formation process by breaking a rotating parent core into smaller masses, and the results show a substantial agreement with the observed mass distribution and spacing patterns. To validate our methodology, we conducted multiple runs by increasing the total mass of the parent core and analyzing the resulting binary systems.

This research presents a novel, efficient implementation of the Independent Component Analysis (ICA) algorithm using GPU architecture, specifically designed for GPU models supporting Coherent Memory Access (e.g. AMD Vega and NVIDIA Turing). By developing a thread-safe algorithm that utilizes contiguous memory access, we achieved significant performance enhancements, reaching speeds of 110.9 MHz, which is 14 times faster than the traditional Python implementation. This optimized ICA code also serves as a starting point for the development of the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm, an innovative method for fast computation of linear models in the Least Squares Method (LSM). The M-ar-K-Fast algorithm was determined to be 17 times faster than the standard Python implementation.

We reevaluate the connection between finite model theory, particularly Choiceless Polynomial Time, and algebraic propositional proof systems like Extended Polynomial Calculus. Our study focuses on distinguishing finite graph properties in Choiceless Polynomial Time and their equivalent counterparts in Evidence Based Inclusion-Exclusion and Semi Algebraic Set Membership. This involves analyzing log-space computable properties of graphs and their associated algebraic and semi-algebraic sets. We also establish a hierarchy of graph properties that are hard to distinguish using polynomial calculus, similar to the Weiermann Big Five but with a distinct structure. This research reveals that the hardness hierarchy for these properties is not simply linear but can exhibit complex patterns.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is additive subgroup closed, under both multiplication and additive morphism is defined as $\sigma$-collection. Ring $R$ is referred to as $\sigma$-ring if the given $\sigma$-collection equals the ring itself in terms of subsets. It has been proven that such a $\sigma$-collection exists in any noncommutative ring with square zero, implying the existence of a subring ideal chain of infinite length within such rings. Furthermore, it has been found that a $\sigma$-ring cannot contain a subring isomorphic to matrix rings over fields, unless the ring itself is isomorphic to such a form. Lastly, it has been proven that the class of $\sigma$-rings satisfies categories such as heredity, stability and and infinite chain stability within the category of rings with zero.

When evaluating claims that have not been disproven, the assessment process can be complicated by a lack of clarity regarding what constitutes evidence or a valid argument structure. In an attempt to organize the reasoning process, a framework for assessing these claims is developed, consisting of a step-by-step evaluation method that identifies and addresses potential weaknesses. Although this approach does not provide a definitive formula for verification, it serves as a guiding principle for the argumentation process and can help identify inconsistencies in the claims made by AI holography researchers.

Emergent incidents such as traffic jams, fires, and accidents can be identified on social media by monitoring related posts. Detecting such incidents in real-time from large volumes of social media data is, however, a complex challenge. Existing solutions rely on rule-based approaches that rely on user tags, which may not always be accurate or available. This work introduces an advanced method for detecting incidents based on geographical and temporal information. It utilizes statistical analysis and machine learning to classify suspicious posts and estimate incident locations. The proposed system effectively detects traffic-related incidents, outperforming rule-based methods by 25-95% in terms of accuracy. It also demonstrates excellent scalability, with a linear complexity allowing it to process over 50,000 posts per second.

A novel, fast, and unbiased technique for analyzing CMB bispectra on small angular scales without requiring computational intensive $N$-body simulations is presented. By accounting for non-Gaussian large-scale structure projections from galaxy surveys and lensing reconstructions, this method enables accurate bispectrum estimation on both small and large scales. The development of this method is motivated by the need to increase the accuracy of CMB lensing reconstructions and galaxy intrinsic alignment estimations by leveraging cross-correlations with the CMB and galaxy lensing bispectra. The method is then applied to estimate the CMB lensing bispectrum and the galaxy intrinsic alignment bispectrum, and these estimates are compared with those obtained using $N$-body simulations.

Machine learning models are particularly vulnerable to manipulation by malicious actors, and our research focuses on developing advanced security measures for Bayesian neural networks. We introduce a novel concept called " adversarial robust Bayesian domains", which comprises samples that are both manipulated by adversaries and uncertain in their classification. Our goal is to create an accurate posterior distribution over the data space, but traditional methods fail to account for the diverse types of manipulated samples. We propose a new method, "Certified Bayesian Unlearn", which leverages convex programming to generate strong guarantees to the worst-case posterior distribution, even in the presence of adversarial manipulation. However, this approach falls short for the "Adversarial Robust Bayesian domains" category. We suggest an alternative framework, "ThreatinGibbs", which offers weaker guarantees but performs well on unlabelled data within such domains. ThreatinGibrs' efficiency is further exemplified through its application in fundamental tasks.

In the initial stage of the pandemic, Chinese social media platforms experienced explosive growth in the spread of rumors. These rumors, reaching up to 12.6% of all posts on Xiaoma, a popular app in China, created significant anxiety among the public and even prompted official action. Researchers developed an algorithm to automatically identify rumors and assess their impact by analyzing retweet patterns. Their model predicted the total number of retweets with high accuracy and identified the top ten factors influencing rumor propagation as follows: the source of the post (80.4% confidence), the time of dissemination (30.4%), the author's credentials (27.7%), the incorporation of credible news sources (25.9%), the incorporation of official news sources (24.5%), the incorporation of health-related information (22.4%), the incorporation of financial information (20.9%), the incorporation of education-related information (19.1%), the incorporation of entertainment information (18.3%), and the incorporation of sports news (16.9%). Researchers demonstrated that by identifying high-risk rumors and their predicted transmission times, early intervention could significantly reduce their spread and associated retweets.

This study investigates the effects of applying various spectral dimensionality reduction techniques to hyperspectral images, focusing on the resulting pixel classification accuracies. A dataset from the ULAAGAN nature reserve in Estonia was used, containing 101 bands from wavelengths 400-1000nm. Our analysis shows that using reduced spectral dimensions in machine learning algorithms does not necessarily impair performance. In fact, certain algorithms remain unaffected by dimensionality reduction, while others see improvements in accuracy with diminished spectral data. A careful examination of the outcomes suggests that the choice of dimensionality reduction technique, pixel classification method, and evaluation metric are interconnected.

Recent research on neural language models has gained significant interest, yet training such models on large datasets is becoming increasingly expensive due to memory and computation constraints. These constraints have led to the concept of authentic language model compression, which aims to decrease the model's computational and memory requirements while preserving its original performance. Our study focuses on this compression of neural language models, including the advancements in the field and our current research in this area. We also introduce a new technique called knowledge distillation with partial model matching (KDM) which can significantly improve the efficiency of authentic language model compression.

A newly developed tool, called ProVerif, uses quantum mechanical calculations to determine the chemical shift of amide protons in proteins by establishing a correlation between chemical shift and the N-H bond length. ProVerif determines chemical shifts with an error margin of less than one standard deviation by considering the complexities of protein environments, thereby enhancing the accuracy in predicting chemical shifts. ProVerif's refinements based on quantum mechanical calculations have proven more effective than conventional methods that rely on empirical formulas, thereby providing a valuable resource for protein structure refinement and validation.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a critical decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions available and the non-convex nature of the optimization problem. Despite this importance, research on loss function optimization often proceeds without thorough examination. Our study aims to investigate how altering loss functions impacts the location, size, and persistence of local minima in binary classification tasks. We utilize two primary metrics: first, the accuracy of final models in predicting test set labels; and second, the consistency of model performance throughout the training process as tracked by metrics like validation set accuracy and generalization loss. Our research employs various loss functions, including modified versions of cross-entropy, KL divergence, and hinge loss, and offers intuitive explanations for the findings.

In this context, we explore the four-point vertex function in the parquet theory through a Hamiltonian-based perspective. By expanding this function in symmetric and antisymmetric components with respect to two indices, we establish a Hamiltonian-driven approach for each part, where the first involves a spin-like model related to a Heisenberg Hamiltonian and the second a model connected to a Léonard-Jones type of interaction, which we term the 'q-photon' model. We discuss how these views contribute to understanding the four-point vertex's nature, particularly its double-summable attribute, and examine the conditions under which it is double-summable. We also investigate the relationship between the two indices and find that one index is associated with particle-particle or particle-hole processes, while the other involves multiple photon processes. Furthermore, we determine that when both indices belong to the same index group, the four-point vertex's double-summability holds under less stringent conditions. We also find that at a finite temperature, the four-point vertex's double-summability is ensured, regardless of the index's origin.

Using a reliable approach that accounts for the dynamic interaction between electrons and photons, we've successfully created and studied exciton condensation in a solid system for the first time. We applied this approach to examine a superconducting transition in 1T-TiSe2, a material that transitions from a normal state to a state containing exciton poles at low temperatures. We found that the dynamic interaction between electrons and photons plays a significant role in triggering the exciton condensation and that the exciton frequencies match predicted values from a theory that considers strong electron interaction effects. We also observed that within a narrow range of electron doses, the exciton condensation gives rise to a type of pairing that can lead to superconductivity. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of a reliable approach for studying exciton condensation in solid systems and provided insights into the complex electron interactions that govern the behavior of materials with strong electron interaction effects.

In recent years, numerous systems for reporting community safety issues through text messaging or online forms have been implemented to facilitate communication between community members and local dispatchers or officials. While these systems appear to primarily serve the purpose of enabling users to submit event descriptions, they actually hold the potential to yield additional valuable information when analyzed more extensively. By aggregating and annotating the full text data submitted via these platforms, officials can gain a more comprehensive understanding of safety concerns within their community, including patterns of recurring incidents, areas experiencing high levels of crime, and the specific types of incidents that require the most attention. This, in turn, can inform the development of more targeted safety initiatives and allocation of resources to effectively address emerging challenges. In this research, we will illustrate the benefits of leveraging full text data from community safety reporting systems, using Los Angeles as a case study.

In the case of unconventional s± superconductors, Cooper pairs with spin of 1 or greater form above a certain low-temperature threshold. Theoretical calculations indicate that Cooper pairs with a spin of 1 or greater exhibit unusual behavior in response to external magnetic fields, particularly intense fields, where magnetic moments associated with spins of 1 or greater become free to move independently. A recent study provides detailed predictions for how Cooper pairs' magnetic moments will behave in response to an external magnetic field in the s± superconductor symmetry type, as well as in response to structural changes within the material. A novel type of paramagnetic response is identified, where the material's magnetic properties decrease in a linear manner with low- to moderate-strength external magnetic fields, providing a potential testing ground for current paramagnetic models of high-temperature superconductors.

We introduce a new framework for digital learning platforms that encourages
users to take an active learning role by minimizing risks in the face of
unreliable feedback from the platform. Traditional learning encouragement
strategies often rely on inaccurate assumptions about users' goals and
predictability. In contrast, our approach develops a game-theoretic model
that assumes users seek to maximize their learning potential while the
platform seeks to minimize learning potential by manipulating risks and
rewarding skeptical decisions. Our framework, called Minimax Engaged Learning,
provides an optimal strategy for players to achieve a mutually beneficial
outcomes and offers practical applications for learning platforms seeking to
balance user education with their own financial gains.

Between 1909 and 2000, the musical statistics of compact discs held by the British Library were analyzed in a previous study. For this current study, additional data from 2000 to 2017 were added to the collection, expanding the analysis to cover the entire period. Song excerpts lasting 35 seconds were taken from randomly selected albums. The analysis measured musical complexity using three different metrics: song variability, melodic range, and chord variability. The results showed that musical complexity continued to decrease over the analyzed period. Compared to the earlier study, this new one covered more albums - 1,932 as opposed to 602 - and included songs across the spectrum of four major record labels: EMI, Sony, Universal, and Warner. The current study's results align with the earlier one's findings, suggesting that musical complexity has been steadily declining for at least 100 years across the popular music of the West.

A novel stochastic process, called the multiple-entry reinforcement process (MERP), is introduced and examined in detail. The MERP is a generalization of the reinforcement process (RP) with multiple entry points, extending the RP's capabilities to simulate a wider range of outcomes. The RP has been applied in various settings, including modeling writer's block and exploring the relationship between frequency and quality in creative production. Our study of the MERP provides a comprehensive analysis of its asymptotic behavior and potentially leads to new applications of this stochastic process in modeling diverse phenomena.

From its inception, the computational interpretation of Ludics has been seen as a major advancement in the field. This advancement led to the development of a duality theory, enabling the examination of model-theoretic and algebraic aspects of Ludics. This research focuses on the harmonic fragments of Ludics, specifically those related to proof systems such as linear logic and beta-reduction. By analyzing these fragments, we gain insights into the core properties of the underlying proof systems as well as their corresponding universal transformations.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data clustering, our method identifies and separates key states and their associated rewards even at low labeling rates, resulting in consistent performance across a range of experiments, even when labeling rates are as low as 5%. Compared to standard methods, our approach saves humans up to 90% time in various scenarios.

We examine Smyth spaces and the core-compactness of their Smyth powerspaces. While a Smyth space's Smyth powerspace is always core-compact, we find that not all core-compact Smyth powerspaces are core-compact. We also provide conditions under which a Smyth space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact.

We're investigating how the interactions of angular vortex loops unfold in ideal two-dimensional fluids. Our research reveals that any interaction results in the loops merging into a single loop, with the exception of certain specific cases where the loops avoid each other's influence without merging. Our findings can be visually represented through the use of a diagram that illustrates the possible outcomes of loop interactions, each characterized by the number of loop splits that occur. This diagram also has connections to the Duality Duality Duality Duality project's findings on game theory.

The average treatment effect can be estimated by AIPW estimators which have two components: a predicted probability of receiving the treatment based on control group data and a prediction model for the outcome. These estimators use an weighting function to standardize the estimates which can be sensitive to model specifications. Recent research suggests using machine learning methods such as neural networks to estimate the standardization probability might be beneficial. By applying these machine learning methods to the control group data instead of the entire data, the AIPW estimators become standardized augmented inverse probability weighting estimators. These new estimators outperformed traditional methods in simulated data and were also used to analyze real world data resulting in more accurate estimates and a 90% reduction in bias compared to standard AIPW estimators.

The behavior of tau leptons is being precisely measured in various tau decays, 
including those involving the emission of electrons or muons. These findings challenge theoretical models of these processes due to anticipated discrepancies between the predictions and the experimental results. Notably, the differential decay rates of tau leptons, particularly when they transition into electrons or muons, are being measured with high accuracy and are expected to deviate significantly from the standard theoretical models by the end of the current measurement process. This expectation raises crucial concerns about the presence of new physics beyond the standard model, particularly in its interaction mechanisms.

A tabletop-sized rotating tank was used to recreate a unique atmospheric and oceanic phenomenon where cold air near the surface meets warm air, causing wave patterns to form at the interface. The tank's rotation further amplifies these patterns, known as baroclinic waves. To assess the effectiveness of two numerical simulation methods - one that models the movement of mass and another that directly solves fluid motion - we compared their results to those obtained through experimental data analysis. The analysis focused on key characteristics of the waves, such as their shapes, frequencies, and behaviors, and revealed notable similarities between the experiments and simulations. Interestingly, small differences in wave patterns began to grow into distinct features as they propagated. Ultimately, understanding the baroclinic wave dynamics in this setup could provide insights into more complex atmospheric and oceanic processes.

A common technique used to model extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this approach offers flexibility in representing extreme events, it can also make Bayesian inference challenging due to issues like posterior computation complexity and the difficulty in interpreting a parameter space that is not continuous. To overcome these problems, a method is proposed that involves transforming the Poisson process parameters into a more manageable and interpretable space. This method also takes into account the effect of extreme event data and can easily be extended for models involving multiple types of extreme events. A numerical example demonstrates the efficiency of this method in performing Bayesian inference for such models.

A reinforcement learning approach known as offline RL can utilize pre-collected datasets to train agents without relying on interactive setup processes. In many scenarios, acquiring a completely pure dataset is extremely difficult; any annotation errors or corruptions can lead to biased policies that cause agents to malfunction post-deployment. Contrary to existing methods that focus solely on robust decision-making in the face of corruption, we introduce an approach to build resilience against corruption throughout the entire offline RL process. Our methodology comprises three key components that address data pre-processing, model development, and value function estimation to counter annotation corruption. Experimental results on a variety of benchmarks indicate that our strategy offers superior outcomes compared to state-of-the-art offline RL methods in the face of corruption.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic concavity of the cost function in relation to the L1-control of the 1-D heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions. Based on this, we prove necessary conditions for optimal controls in a unique Pontryagin-type maximum principle framework. The study further establishes sufficient conditions for optimal controls in a regular dependence framework. The key ideas in proving logarithmic concavity involve exploiting the sub-marginal growth equation in a specific dual system and leveraging a comparison result for a related decoupled linear parabolic problem.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We address this ambiguity by categorizing and analyzing the diverse nature of out-of-distribution texts. It is discovered that existing detection methods are ineffective against a particular group of out-of-distribution examples which are commonly found in real-world scenarios. A new dataset, called FBankDec, is developed to facilitate the research on out-of-distribution example detection in language models. It is comprised of 434,111 French sentences that are unclear due to poor audio quality. We also introduce a new approach for out-of-distribution example detection, called STO, which is effective against all identified types of out-of-distribution examples including those in the FBankDec dataset.

This study examines molecular motors powered by intermittent electron leakage, investigating the complex dynamics resulting from the competition between this leakage and the subsequent resonant energy absorption. The investigation focuses on Brownian molecular engines characterized by five states, with the exception of one which is off-grid, and based on the Cohen-Kundu-Mukherjee model. The analysis takes into consideration both the influence of tunneling and resonant energy absorption as well as their combination. The findings show that in the absence of tunneling, the system displays periodic motion, but when only tunneling is considered, the system becomes chaotic. However, when resonant energy absorption is factored in, the system's dynamics changes drastically, displaying stable cycles and chaos borders are replaced with stable cycles. The investigation also finds that when both tunneling and resonant energy absorption are competing, the system can exist in various stable cycle states, achieved by adjusting a few control parameters. The study discovers that at a specific parameter setting, the system's motion becomes periodic once more. The only condition for this periodic motion is that the rate of tunneling must be slower than the rate of resonant energy absorption.

Building on a 2014 framework, we expand the concept of synchronizing systems in terms of their transition structures. Focusing on word transducers, which can be viewed as a specific type of transition systems, we establish a criterion for a non-complete idempotent system to become recognizable and effective under specific conditions. Furthermore, this criterion yields a new complexity classification for directionally regular word transducers with a single direction of operation. The resulting complexity classifications are either $n^{O\log n}$ or $2^{n}.

In this research, we explore new possibilities for computing the generalized convolution (also known as the sum of products, SOP) function more efficiently, through novel approaches that don't rely on existing factorization methods like ESOP and AC. Our findings show that under specific conditions, the generalized convolution can be calculated faster than the current fastest known sequential algorithms. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a circuit contains a limited number of two input variables within a specific sub-circuit, known as a small monogene sub-circuit, we can compute the generalized convolution for that sub-circuit in logarithmic time, a significant improvement over the previous best efforts. Building on this discovery, we developed two new algorithms, one for each type of circuit structure, that allow us to compute the generalized convolution in logarithmic time, a major advancement over the previous best efforts.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its formation and evolution process, yet its spectral characteristics remained unclear, especially in the mid-spectral range. Employing the APOLLO retrieval code to analyze observational data of GJ 229B and T/Y brown dwarfs, researchers successfully obtained precise spectra and temperature constraints for GJ 229B. Notably, the analysis indicates water and ammonia clouds prevail on or above the location of the NH$_3$ optical absorption band's formation, which also identifies carbon-bearing clouds as key emitters of infrared emission in the system. By comparing models and observations, researchers find a discrepancy of about 100 K for GJ 229B's temperature, emphasizing the necessity of time-resolved spectroscopic observations to clarify the system's carbon geometry.

To describe the behavior of the negative-parity JPC state 0^--, we need to incorporate terms containing the $\vec{E}$.\$\vec{E}$ structure, specifically those involving the electric form factor, into the wave function. Utilizing the method of radial Hilbert transforms to calculate form factors, our approach allows for the systematic study of interactions via complex form factors. Our preliminary findings suggest that the 0^-- state could be potentially observable in experiments with specific energy thresholds, as we discuss the relevance of potential technical difficulties and how to address them.

A review of the theoretical and experimental progress in studying $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ is presented. These quantities, crucial for understanding $\phi_s$ and the scalar-to-vector current ratio, are essential for determining the CKM angle $\gamma$ and testing R_b. The role of $\phi_s$ in studying these parameters is discussed, along with the challenges and prospects of LHCb's ongoing and future research.

Airborne transmission risk in enclosed environments like buses is quantified using a modeling approach that assumes turbulent air mixing. This assessment considers various factors such as virus infectivity, air exchange rates, and passenger respiratory behaviors. By applying this model to a typical urban bus, the risk of airborne transmission is calculated for different passenger configurations and virus droplet sizes. Specifically, the analysis explores how different assumptions about virus size affect overall transmission risk. Furthermore, a sensitivity study is conducted to investigate how various factors like virus infectivity, air exchange rates, and respiratory factors influence transmission risk.

This study has performed large-scale shell-model calculations for the $\beta$-decay properties of $^{135,137}$Te nuclei, focusing on the neutrinoless capture process. Researchers have computed the absolute $\beta$-decay half-lives and the electron antineutrino-outgoing partial $\beta$ decay rates of these nuclei. Comparing their results with experimental data, the researchers found reasonable agreement, considering the inherent uncertainties in the nuclear Hamiltonian. Using the SIC-SDSM approach, the researchers estimated the neutrinoless capture rates of $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te as 1.3$\times$10$^{-13}$ and 1.1$\times$10$^{-13}$ s$^{-1}$, respectively. The researchers believe that future experiments with improved sensitivity may be able to detect the sign of the neutrinoless capture process in $^{137}$Te.

Double Sided Auctions are being adopted in various applications due to their
efficiency in matching demand and supply. However, the presence of malicious
parties in such environments poses a threat to the correct functioning of the
system, an issue not yet thoroughly explored in the literature. This paper
addresses the security concerns of Double Sided Auctions by introducing a new
protocol that ensures the participants' privacy and the integrity of the system
against cheating activities. The proposed algorithm is proven to be secure
against a malicious auctioneer and participants in separate attacks, and its
efficiency is verified through real-world experimentation. Furthermore, this
paper provides comprehensive empirical analysis of the Double Sided Auctions
tilling problem, including results on the optimal prices, and offers a range of
experimentally validated metrics to evaluate algorithm performance.

Utilizing heavy quark effective theory and perturbative QCD, we investigate the properties of F-wave bottom mesons, calculating their mass and decay constant in terms of a form factor. We further evaluate the decay width of certain bottom meson transitions and discuss the relevance of linear confinement within this context.

J Journey and M Morin initially demonstrated in their work "Commuting and periodic graphs" that every complete graph of order at least three can be expressed as the result of the product of two commuting bipartite graphs along with a cycle graph. Later, in their follow-up research "Commuting and complete graphs", they showed that this statement holds true for all complete graphs. Our present paper extends these findings by stating that every cyclic graph can be represented as the result of the product of two commuting bipartite graphs along with a complete graph. Additionally, we establish a method for identifying periodic graphs, which involves breaking them down into complete graphs and bipartite graphs. We also introduce a straightforward algorithm for finding the shortest path in the metric graph, where adjacent vertices are connected by edges of length one, and show that this graph exhibits expander properties.

We introduce a data-driven method for learning robust dynamics models in complex systems with potential biases and errors in data sampling. Our approach builds upon the dynamic mode decomposition technique by incorporating optimization algorithms to develop a suitable kernel function for the dynamics model. We apply kernel learning techniques to identify an optimal nonlinear function, which enhances the accuracy and robustness of the models. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to various physical systems with different objective functions, as demonstrated in two numerical simulations and one experimental case study.

Utilizing data from the chess-focused subreddit r/chess, we analyzed the intricacy and connection strength of various chess opening patterns by adapting complex network methods. Our analysis categorized 34 distinct opening types into four levels of intricacy, with control as the least complex and 1e4 as the most complex. Additionally, we mapped different chess opening patterns to the standard Stockfish notation used by chess players and found significant correlations between the frequency of these patterns and player success levels, with more intricate openings generally associated with higher-skilled players. Our study also discovered that the top-performing players on lichess.org prefer less complex openings, while novice players on chess.com tend to use more intricate openings. These findings align with existing research on chess player strategies.

This research explores the potential of advanced red giant branches or asymptotic giant branch stars to create black holes through the process of accretion-induced collapse, and the resulting black holes can then coalesce with neutron stars to form millisecond pulsars. We've developed a reliable method for calculating the fundamental parameters of these pulsars, such as their rotational periods and spin velocities, and the resulting masses after the coalescence event. Our approach involves preliminary estimates of the red giant's mass and luminosity, followed by calculations of the neutron star's initial velocity and the final black hole-mass-pulsar radius correlation. We've applied this framework to a specific binary system composed of a 0.03 solar mass dwarf and a neutron star with a 2-day orbital period, in which the dwarf star is assumed to have undergone accretion-induced collapse and then interacted with the neutron star. Our calculations reveal a final black hole-mass-pulsar radius of approximately 13.9 solar radii, and the resulting millisecond pulsar is expected to have a rotational period of about 16.8 days and a spin velocity of 884 km/s. Our findings align with existing data and the observed trends in the black hole-mass-pulsar radius correlation, and we expect that future surveys will uncover numerous systems like this one.

A general method to derive the Euler equations of any order for a Lagrangian model with a nonlocal component has been developed. From this, an expression for the corresponding'momenta of motion' is obtained, along with which we investigate specific cases, beginning with the order of Lagrangian dynamics being two, for both a discrete and a continuous system. We further generalize our approach by obtaining the equations of motion for the entire set of'moments of motion'. This involves considering a discrete system of Lagrangian maps with higher order impacts, and then a continuous system described by a Yang-Mills type theory. The results show that the'moments of motion' lead to a more comprehensive understanding of the conservation laws.

This study introduces an innovative task that enables users to create three-dimensional objects in virtual reality (VR) and utilize sketches of existing 3D shapes to retrieve similar models from a large database. We have developed a comprehensive system to support this task, consisting of a virtual drawing tool and an advanced retrieval method. The virtual drawing tool allows users to freely create three-dimensional shapes in VR, while our retrieval method leverages deep learning and graph search to effectively utilize three-dimensional shape features for more accurate retrievals. We have conducted user studies in both VR and 2D environments to evaluate the created shapes and our retrieval approach, achieving promising results and gathering valuable insights for future developments.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in heat as it approaches the inner edge of its orbit due to its extremely eccentric path. As the planet rapidly spins at the speed of 3000 km/h, its surface temperature shifts dramatically within hours, presenting an extraordinary environment that could support the presence of atmospheric escape, cloud formation, and other dynamic phenomena. Recent observations by the James Webb Space Telescope are expected to shed light on the planet's atmospheric evolution. To accurately plan these observations, the position of HD80606b needs to be known in advance with great precision. To achieve this, our research team conducted a thorough analysis of the planet's movement around its host star, utilizing a wide network of telescopes that allow for continuous monitoring of the planet as it orbits the star. By examining the changes in the star's brightness caused by the planet's passage, we were able to refine the planet's movement and schedule a series of observations that ensure the effective planning of JWST research missions.

In this investigation, we examine spherically symmetric, non-rotating isentropic collapses from a point mass in a D-dimensional space, assuming a linear relationship between pressure and density. We show that in a 4D space, such collapses result in a permanent singularity, whereas in a higher-dimensional space (D>4), we successfully derive a radiative solution that matches the Schwarzschild solution at large distances. We also discuss how the equation of state influences the stability and behavior of collapse, including a special case where a previously unknown solution to the Einstein equations is presented.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the outcomes of extreme black holes based on initial data and perturbations. This method has been effectively applied to calculate first and second-order corrections for both conserved and non-conserved charges in various scenarios. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that when the perturbations vanish, our corrections align with existing results, thereby validating our approach.

A key aspect of motor skill development involves identifying the outcomes produced by unknown relationships between actions and their consequences.
This outcome detection capability is essential for creatures to learn new skills.
We propose a simple computational model of motor learning that can learn complex skills in dynamic environments with changing obstacles as long as they consistently produce similar effects.
Our study demonstrates that a robotic arm controlled by a neural network can be taught to develop a reliable driving strategy to reach a goal by sampling motion paths and predicting the resulting positions.
Through trial-and-error, the robot learns to connect its actions to the end positions, using this knowledge to guide future movements even when the environment changes.

A generalized action of Poincaré symmetry in a higher-dimensional spacetime has been formulated. This enhanced algebra incorporates additional vectors from the Lee-Tang tensor. The beauty of the Poincaré symmetry lies in its ability to seamlessly integrate gravity and the actions of massive and massless particles within a unified framework. The novel approach emerges when the Poincaré symmetry is generated from the flat spacetime's general coordinate transformations via a dimensional reduction technique. This method remarkably reveals that the Poincaré symmetry action is a straightforward combination of the particle's action and the Einstein-Hilbert action for gravity. The findings provide a pathway for developing a widespread concept of Poincaré symmetry, which could lead to significant insights in both gravity and particle physics.

Designing parameterized algorithms for complex problems is a crucial area of study, particularly when simpler heuristics fail to deliver satisfactory results. In graph theory, upward planarity, which involves visualizing a graph in a upward direction while avoiding edge crossings, is a problem that often lacks adequate solutions. This study focuses on developing new parameterized techniques to tackle this challenge. Specifically, it introduces a set of parameters that can help simplify the problem and proposes several algorithmic solutions based on these parameters. The paper also attempts to define the complexity of these problems and identifies new NP-complete classes in the realm of planar graphs.

Image-based goal navigation datasets typically provide extensive training, 
but pose challenges in inference due to the need to store and recall numerous 
image memories. Our approach, MemoNav, addresses this by developing an 
efficient method to capture relevant environmental details during navigation, 
thus reducing the need to store every encountered image. MemoNav involves a 
complex network of recurrent transformers that process both agent and sensor 
observations, and includes a query transformer to identify and prioritize 
relevant memories from the collected trajectory. Our experiments demonstrate 
MemoNav's superiority over baseline methods that store every encountered image 
or use simplified environmental encoders, particularly in navigation tasks with 
limited training data.

Small cells have been a cornerstone in mobile networks for addressing coverage and data rate issues since their introduction in 3G CDMA technology. They have continued to evolve with each new mobile technology, with LTE providing significant enhancements in terms of cost, efficiency, and flexibility. This article summarizes the history and advancements of small cell technology from 2G to 6G, highlighting key developments in each phase and the existing research in each area. The article also identifies ongoing challenges and explores future possibilities in small cell technology.

This tutorial focuses on dynamic network systems where both network topology and dynamical node behavior are undefined, but can be estimated from partial information. A statistical framework is developed to address both tasks simultaneously. The results are capable of handling significant data noise and are adaptable to various types of network data. The method is extensively evaluated using artificial data sets and applied to analyze real-world networks consisting of brain activity, cell metabolism, and social media interactions.

Building on the connection between growth of operators and classical probability spaces, we develop a general framework to examine the relationship between growth patterns in quantum systems. This theoretical framework, represented by a specific type of operator algebra, enables us to study the distinct growth patterns exhibited by quantum states and their relationship with the systems' degrees of freedom. This is achieved by integrating various approaches, incorporating techniques from noncommutative probability theory, operator algebras, and quantum information. Utilizing this comprehensive framework, we investigate specific patterns of growth in random quantum systems, including those found in quantum Gaussian systems and SO(q) symmetric systems, and analyze their distinct characteristics in terms of operator connectivity and complexity. This analysis sheds light on how operator connectivity and complexity behave in different growth patterns and whether they converge as the system size increases.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV within the $0^+$_{1} 0.615 MeV level in $^{12}$C, has been a topic of interest for a long time due to its unusual properties. The Hoyle state primarily decays into the $^{8}$Be+$\alpha$ channel but also undergoes ground-state decay into the $^{8}$Be+ n+ proton. Researchers have recently developed an experimental technique using a Time-Projection Chamber to quantify the partial decay width of the Hoyle state into the $^{8}$Be+ n+ proton channel. The analysis of the data shows that 49± 7% of the Hoyle state decays through the $^{8}$Be+ n+ proton channel with the partial decay width of 1.01± 0.15 keV. The newly determined ratio joins other studies in refining our understanding of the Hoyle state decay pattern.

A numerical study conducted pressure tests dynamic fracture in 2D models of brittle materials, revealing the emergence of underlined scales due to intrinsic material properties. In such scenarios, stress oscillations at a specific wavelength frequently occur, leading to either a shift in fracture direction or a fracture tip splitting phenomenon. The underlying mechanism responsible for these oscillations involves a competition between stress relaxation and the propagation of elastic waves within the material. The onset of the most prominent instability mode is shown to be a result of the inherent material length scales present in the stress singularity. The following lengths scales are examined in this study: the critical length scale (R$_0$) associated with stress concentration, the intrinsic length scale (R$_f$) associated with fracture energy, and the intrinsic length scale (R$_p$) associated with polymer-like brittle materials. The study demonstrates that the ratio of R$_f$/R$_p$ can be a crucial indicator for fracture splitting or propagation changes. The study further observes that the fracture splitting mode can propagate in a dynamic fracture process and highlights the significance of understanding the intrinsic material length scales in fracture dynamics.

We investigate the fundamental limits of reliable communication in a network with a specific structure, where a transmitter is connected to receivers via channels with complex internal structures and dynamic behaviors, influenced by previous transmissions and reception histories. The transmitter has access to complete information about its internal state, while receivers only have limited information about the transmitter's state. Our study focuses on the specific case when all channels involved are finite-state Markov chains. We develop a framework for achieving optimal error rates by leveraging data from past transmission and reception events. The proposed approach is then applied to two key scenarios: when the transmitter has complete information and when only a part of the information is accessible. For these cases, we derive achievable rate limits and outline relevant coding techniques. The results show that when the transmitter has complete information, it is possible to reach an optimal error rate of $Q^*$ (defined as the minimum error probability when using an optimal coding strategy without consideration of past transmissions). When only part of the information is accessible, we establish a lower bound on the optimal error rate and demonstrate that it can approach $Q^*$ if the available information sufficient enough. The proposed coding strategies are shown to be effective in reaching these optimal error rates in both scenarios.

In a theoretical study, researchers investigated the presence of topological superfluidity in a 2D system consisting of spin-1/2 Rashba orbitals coupled by both spin-conserving and spin-flip interactions with an adjacent grid of nodes. Pseudospin polarizability and long-range pairing due to spin-orbit coupling led to the formation of spin-singlet pairs with angular momentum, which is a necessary characteristic for topological superconductivity. Utilizing a sign structure from the SU(2) symmetric point as a guide, researchers constructed a model of Majorana ribbons and demonstrated the appearance of zero-energy modes in odd-shaped systems with specified boundaries of filling. Finite-size numerical analyses confirmed this prediction, also revealing that topological superfluidity in this system is resistant to repulsive interactions that destroy it in more general scenarios.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables within scientific research papers. We have developed two new challenges for the SemEval 2021 competition centered on fact verification and evidence identification for tabular data. The first task requires assessing whether a statement is supported by a given table, considering columns as data fields. We received 48 submissions for this task. The second task involves locating the actual evidence in a table for a given statement, with participants able to utilize additional context from the surrounding paper context. Due to limited participation, we did not hold a competition for task 2. We have made all participating data available for future research purposes.

This analysis explores the pivotal role of complex numbers in quantum mechanics, delving into their necessity and examining alternative number systems that might be considered as potential substitutes for complex numbers in quantum modeling. Although the discussion is generally focused, specific attention is given to the connection between complex numbers and the principles of quantum entanglement and the Pauli equations.

A graph metric dimension is its smallest cardinality of a set of distinct vertices whose positions are sufficient for locating every other vertex by computing the minimum distance. We introduce a generalized concept - the k-trimmed metric dimension - where a subset of vertices can eliminate at most k vertices' locations, and aim to find optimal such subsets for specific tree shapes.
These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a class.

This work has examined methods to effectively eliminate sulfur oxides from post combustion flue gas through chemical oxidation using ozone. Previous studies identified UV-light as a means to enhance the oxidation process by increasing the collision rate of molecules. Building on this, various UV lamp configurations were tested for their potential in integrating the removal system. A study on energy efficiency led to the discovery that using multiple small lamps in series achieved the best SOx removal rate. A numerical model was developed to simulate the oxidation process and results aligned perfectly with experimental findings. A design scheme for a full-scale installation has been proposed based on the optimal configuration of UV lamps in reactors.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in testing and evaluating this innovative hardware platform. To overcome this obstacle, developers are leveraging advanced design tools to create realistic simulations of the system, its interactions, and data flows before actual prototypes exist. In this work, we present a novel simulation environment based on SystemC for simulating neuromorphic computing systems. Our approach incorporates multiple modeling techniques to ensure accuracy and speed. Specifically, we employ transactional programming for accurate event handling and a concurrent VPSIM model for efficient data processing. Furthermore, we develop a reusable framework for simulating complex systems, thereby enabling rapid modifications and variations. Our simulation framework is thoroughly tested and validated through various use cases, demonstrating its effectiveness in supporting education, research, and development endeavors.

Machine learning models known as Indecision Trees can argue in an adversarial manner, opposing each other on classification issues, and are resistant to manipulation because their arguments remain consistent and cannot be altered easily. However, these models have some limitations; they only work well with binary data and only predict simple outcomes. To tackle these issues, we developed a more advanced model called the InDecision Forest, which builds on the work of the Indecision Tree. The InDecision Forest has several key features. First, it can classify complex outcomes more accurately. Second, it can handle information that is incomplete or contains errors. Third, it can learn even when the available data is limited. Finally, it can make more informed predictions when there is noisier data. We tested the InDecision Forest using several real-world datasets and compared its performance to that of other machine learning models, including those that can learn under uncertain conditions. Our results show that the InDecision Forest performs as well as or better than the other models in a variety of scenarios.

The DTW distance measure is widely employed for comparing time series, but its high computational cost renders it ineffective for large-scale similarity search tasks. Several strategies have been devised to enhance performance, including data reduction techniques like dimensionality reduction and random projection, as well as early discarding methods that terminate the DTW computation before its completion. Our research builds upon these approaches by integrating pruned DTW and early discarding, yielding superior results in large-scale similarity search experiments. Moreover, we propose an optimized early discarding strategy, dubbed EDP-ED, which surpasses the performance of recently developed state-of-the-art methods.

Current educational tools in software testing, such as Testimons, have primarily focused on promoting student code testing through rewards for improving code quality. However, past studies have revealed that this approach may have negative effects on student motivation and learning. To address these concerns, our empirical investigation examines the outcomes of using either Inquire-Based Conceptual Feedback or traditional thorough feedback methods in a introductory computing course. Key findings show that students receiving Inquire-Based Conceptual Feedback demonstrated lower levels of motivation, but performed similarly in terms of learning outcomes when compared to the traditional thorough feedback group. A closer analysis of student perceptions towards testing and the feedback mechanism reveals significant differences.

In recent years, the reliability of machine learning models in high-stakes decision-making has been questioned due to a lack of understandability. Therefore, there is a growing need for methods that can provide users with insights into the decision-making processes of these models. This study explores the feasibility of combining the strengths of three approaches - Conceptual Analysis, explanation learning, and constraint-based learning - to fully comprehend the internal workings of machine learning models, particularly those based on deep neural networks. By integrating these methods, we propose a novel technique for generating explicit, interpretable models and expert-like explanations for CNNs, DNNs, and ENNs, as demonstrated through an empirical evaluation using the MNIST dataset.

Deep learning methods have become the preferred choice for graph representation learning, with the Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) being a highly popular choice. Despite its widespread adoption, there has been a lack of investigation into the boundary over-smoothing phenomenon in GCN. In our paper, we delve into the inner workings of GCN and demonstrate that the network's capabilities gradually decline as the network thickness increases. Furthermore, we quantify the GCN's representational capacity by analyzing the eigenvalues of the normalized adjacency matrix. Based on our findings, we propose two novel strategies to enhance the discriminative ability of thick GCN networks. Experimental results show that our proposed methods outperform thinner baselines and achieve state-of-the-art performance in various benchmarks.

A search for dark matter or an abnormal value of the neutrino helicity flavour parameter $\xi_\mathrm{h}$ was conducted using data collected by the CMS experiment from proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy, resulting in the creation of Z bosons that decayed into electrons or muons. The Z bosons had low energy levels, which required a search focus on the Z boson's helicity flavour parameter $\xi_\mathrm{h}$ or dark matter production in association with a Z boson. The study used a dataset of nearly 82 million proton-proton interactions, which is equivalent to a luminosity of 17.4 inverse femtobarns. The Z boson candidate events were classified into three groups based on the Z boson candidate mass, range, and charge. The Z boson candidate events were then compared to the standard model predictions, which revealed an excess in one group of Z boson candidate events that has a 3.4 sigma difference from the standard model predictions. The Z boson candidate events with an excess in the mass range of approximately 1.0 to 1.8 TeV were also searched for dark matter production, which did not have any significant differences from the standard model predictions. The Z boson candidate events with an excess in the mass range of approximately 1.0 to 1.8 TeV were used to set new limits on the cross section of the standard model interactions between the proton and

We propose several new distribution functions dependent on $k_\perp$ in addition to $f_{\rm gl}^{\,<\>}$, and discuss their properties as well as relationships with existing functions such as $f_{\rm gl}^{\,<\>}$, $f_{\rm p}^{\,<\>}$, and $f_{\rm a}^{\,<\>}$, particularly in the context of fast hadronization.

Homeomorphisms of a $T_0$ compact space can be given a topological structure that is a locally compact topological group. This paper provides a characterization of when the homeomorphisms of a $T_0$ compact space form a locally compact topological group. It is known that any locally compact topological group that is homeomorphic to a compact space can be realized as the group of homeomorphisms of a compact space. Building on previous work, the current paper determines which compact spaces their respective groups of homeomorphisms form locally compact topological groups. The characterization involves the application of the Cohen-Killing graph, a combinatorial structure that reflects the topological properties of compact spaces with locally compact homeomorphism groups. The study includes examples and implications for the theory of compact abelian groups and the classification of finite-dimensional locally compact groups.

Research into remote epitaxy on graphene substrates is highly active due to
