the minimal involvement of graphene in the crystal structure and the possibility of
producing high-quality crystals with reduced defects. Nevertheless, the precise
mechanisms through which graphene exerts its influence on crystal growth are still
being investigated. This study explores the variation in film growth modes
exemplified by the Kondo effect in ferromagnetic Heusler films grown on graphene,
utilizing in-situ reflection high-energy electron diffraction for real-time data
collection. By adjusting the substrate temperature and molecular beam power,
different epitaxial relationships were achieved and their corresponding electronic
properties were observed. This discovery indicates that the epitaxial relationship
can be chosen based on the necessity to either minimize defects or exploit the
benefits of remote epitaxy by leveraging temperature as a controlling factor.

We analyze how to make reliable forecasts for key statistics in multivariate time series data when there's limited information available from prior observations. Our method is particularly effective when dealing with unusual events and provides accurate results up to a certain error margin without the need to estimate heavy-tailed distributions. The approach is then demonstrated using real-world data on stock prices and network traffic.

Recent JWST observations of El Gordo, the massive galaxy cluster, have identified a distant red giant star located far beyond the cluster's foreground. To analyze this discovery, the authors employed JWST data to map the cluster's gravitational lensing effects and developed a new model for El Gordo based on its distorted light pattern. By using this model to correct the JWST spectrum, the authors estimated the position of the outlier star and found that it is located at approximately z ~ 0.85. To verify their model, the authors compared it to the results from the JWST F210B channel observation and also used it to verify the redshift z ~ 0.87 for the star identified by the machine learning algorithm, LDA. The authors also used their model to verify the redshift z ~ 0.87 for the star identified by the machine learning algorithm, LDA, and found good agreement. To verify their model, the authors compared it to the results from the JWST F210B channel observation and found good agreement. By using their model, the authors estimated an accurate position for the star located far beyond the cluster and found that its position corresponds roughly to the location of the SPT-CL J0102$-$4915 central bright galaxy. The authors used their model to verify the redshift z ~ 0.87 for the star identified by the machine learning algorithm, LDA, and found good agreement.

The rising demand for online content and rising network access costs have prompted content distributors to enter agreements with internet service providers, who in return, prioritize their traffic. These profit sharing contracts are contingent upon the internet service provider successfully prioritizing the content under a Quality of Service agreement. If the agreement is unsuccessful, the content distributor is not obligated to pay the agreed-upon profits. In this research, we develop a mathematical model based on these contracts and apply stochastic dynamic programming to determine the optimal pricing for content distributors and internet service providers. Our findings also compare the results to two alternative scenarios: a scenario in which profits are guaranteed but not reflected in pricing, and a scenario in which no contracts are established based on the current status quo. The research uses real-world price data to evaluate the outcomes.

The GNS construction builds a Hilbert space from a C*-algebra state and an observable, offering an essential tool for reconstructing physical systems from their underlying mathematical framework. By treating unitary equivalence as a 2-categorical relationship, we demonstrate that the GNS construction itself becomes a unitary equivalence invariant method for associating a Hilbert space with a C*-algebra. Specifically, this involves establishing a 2-categorical construction that includes the standard GNS construction as a special case. Furthermore, we show that the reverse process, taking a Hilbert space back to its original C*-algebra, can be achieved through a functor that represents the equivalence of the 2-construction category.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in cosmology involve a series of symmetries that can be realized in global form as $\mathbb{Z}_2$ or $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ groups. These models feature a set of gauged $SO(p) \times SO(5-p)$ symmetries in a framework that incorporates an $\mathbb{Z}_2$-invariant supergravity theory. The attraction of these models lies in their ability to be tested experimentally: the transition to the de Sitter phase can be matched to the predictions of inflationary models with cascading potentials, while the $\alpha$-attractor mechanism allows for a wide range of target spaces and gauged symmetries to be analyzed. Our research delves into the characteristics of various models associated with different types of symmetries and offers a comprehensive evaluation of the resulting cosmological models, including those related to $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ groups. We also discuss the potential issues with previously proposed models and provide a unified perspective on the subject, presenting multiple examples of cosmological models and their predictions for future observational missions like CMB-S4.

For quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic surfaces that deviate slightly from the Fuchsian surface, our research finds that their measured foliations at infinity remain nearly flat, requiring an error bound of O(q^((1/2)+k/2)) where k is the dimension of the surface's boundary and q controls the deviation. This error estimate includes the constant k/2, which cannot be eliminated despite taking the limit q to zero. Our approach employs the small dilation operator initially proposed by M\"oller and then extended by others, along with finite rank projections over the space of square integrable functions on the upper horizontal boundary of the tree-like domain formed by identifying pairs of boundary components under a small dilation.

This study endeavors to simplify existing methodologies for evaluating manager performance by bridging the gap between theoretical model-based metrics and freely available, easily interpretable measures like alpha and Sharpe ratio. In addition to its methodological contributions, the research also examines real-world performance metrics in detail.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and listening to heart sounds has long been a vital part of a doctor's examination. However, automatic analysis of these sounds has been hindered by complex background noise and the distorted recordings often found in large databases. To tackle these issues, this paper proposes a robust classification approach for heart sounds in the statistics of temporal difference domain. It's been tested using data from the MIT-BIH dataset and real patient recordings, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in handling noisy signals and distorted recordings.

We've considered interactions between $^{133}$Cs and new particles beyond the Standard Model, assuming the presence of four types of new physics: left-handed, right-handed coupling with a specific CP orientation, and two separate CP orientations with equal left and right couplings. The atomic data, combined with experiments on electron scattering and the muon anomalous magnetic moment, reveal the following constraints on the energy scale $\Lambda$ of the new interactions: for a specific type of interaction, $\Lambda$ is constrained between $3.8\times10^3$ and $1.2\times10^5$ GeV, while interactions with different CP orientations have corresponding constraints of a similar magnitude. These new constraints are further discussed in relation to the energy scale $\Lambda$ of the new interactions.

This work examines twisted versions of the torus function, considering transformations imposed by 2-dimensional crystallographic point groups. For each of the 17 possible point groups, we compute the twisted function's symmetries and determine its orbital angular momentum. By combining these results, we construct a classification system for the twisted torus function across all 17 point groups.

This analysis explores how geography and climate influence the development and
characterization of communal relationships within societies that inhabit varied
natural environments. Utilizing a data set comprising 1,018 societies from around
the world, we quantify the impact of climate, terrain features, and population
sizes on the formation and intensity of communal bonds. Our results reveal that
societies residing in areas with mild climate and diverse natural resources tend
to experience minimal social fragmentation and increased cooperation among group
members. Conversely, populations living in harsh environments with limited
available resources are more likely to experience social fragmentation and less
cooperative behavior within their groups.

This study introduces a class of time-scale based manipulators called fractional series manipulators, which operate within the framework of discrete Hardy spaces. The product of a robotic arm's link is modeled using the Frounessser operator, an important abstraction in time-scale calculus. The manipulator's point is represented by a signal in the discrete Hardy space, and its trajectory can be generated by translating this point in three-dimensional space. The objective of this work is to derive efficient algorithms for calculating the robotic arm's equations of motion, as well as its kinematic and dynamic models, all of which are based on the Frounessser operator.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of trustworthiness in second-price auctions through a rigorous laboratory experiment. Our unique setup enables bidders to form expectations about the likelihood of opposing bidders underpromising. Our results demonstrate that the standard auction equilibrium predicts bidder behavior with remarkable accuracy, even when bidders' perceptions of underpromising diverge from its actual probability. Additionally, we find that the frequency of trustworthiness exceeds chance, occurring nearly 56% of the time. Our data further reveal that losses incurred by untrustworthy bidders are significantly higher than those of their trustworthy counterparts. Ultimately, our experiment's outcomes support the prevalence of trustworthiness in auctions, implying that a simple rule encouraging bidders to assume underpromising is a reliable strategy for maximizing profits.

The explanation of gravitational phenomena is enhanced by a novel theory called $f(Q)$-gravity, where the quadratic field $Q$ in torsion replaces the Palatini approach's spin connection. We examine how this theory's symmetry breaking affects physically vital parameters, such as isotropy, in locally rotationally symmetric Bianchi-I universes. Our research focuses on two specific $f(Q)$-gravity models and derived systematic behavioral patterns for different types of cosmological configurations. We found that in both models, when the torsion's impact is dominant, a big universe naturally becomes isotropic, albeit asymptotically. Our findings indicate that in both theories, a big universe naturally becomes isotropic, albeit asymptotically, which supports the theory's validity.

We establish an explicit relationship between three objects: the local defining ring at a specific point on a nilpotent Hessenberg variety, a particular type of Gröbner basis, and a specific type of partition. This understanding is achieved through a decomposition of the Hessenberg variety into smaller components called its standard geometric vertices. By analyzing the local defining ring, we can calculate the dimensions of the varieties for all Hessenberg matrices, and our method also allows us to identify a set of parameters that determine the Gröbner basis. Additionally, our work connects the Hessenberg variety to another geometric object called a torus, and we show that the subvarieties resulting from the division of the Hessenberg variety by its standard geometric vertices are all non-degenerate. We also find a specific type of combinatorial object, called the Frobenius k-partitions, which plays a significant role in this study.

Painting, a art form that has been around for centuries, requires an intuitive understanding of color relationships and visual coherence. Machine learning has made significant advancements in generating paintings, but most previous efforts relied on generated images from text descriptions or used external datasets as a starting point for brushstrokes. A painting's overall aesthetic effect is best captured by its overall appearance and color scheme, rather than the individual strokes. A neural network is proposed that takes a description in the form of text and produces a painting through a two-stage process: initially, a color palette is created based on the description, and then the palette is used to generate the final artwork through iterative adjustments. The network is named Delight, and it outperforms other painting generation models by producing more visually appealing results, according to both objective metrics and human evaluation.

We present an one-parameter model where a single scalar field, coupled with a light pseudoscalar field, can explain the observed anomalies in $K$ and $B$ meson systems, such as the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly in $K$ decays and the $B^+$$\to$$K^+$$\pi^0$ $\mathcal{B}(K^0_{\ell+}$$\to$$K^0\ell^+$ branching ratio in $B^+$$\to$$K^+$$\pi^0$ decays. The proposed theory involves vectorlike top-partner states that are near the kinematic threshold, and the Regime of the Composite Pseudoscalar Phases, a three-fold degenerate minimum in the theory, sets the mass scale for the heavy hadronic system. The predicted masses for several mesons, including the $\pi^0$-like state, are found to be in the several hundred MeV range. The model's predictions for several direct particle collider searches, including those for $K$ and $B$ systems, are also discussed. The specific search for $K^0_{\ell+}$$\to$$K^0\ell^+$ in $B^+$$\to$$K^+$$\pi^0$ decays is found to be challenging but feasible to test in upcoming experiments.

When users engage with scientific literature, they frequently pose questions that require in-depth knowledge of specific subjects. However, current NLP systems are not designed to handle such complex inquiries, leading to missed opportunities for NLP model improvement. To bridge this gap, we have developed a large dataset of 54K Q&A pairs focusing on topics like hyperglycemia, cancer cell biology, and neurodegenerative diseases, all grounded in 2.5K biomedical research papers. Our dataset is comprised of Q&A pairs from two types of text: abstracts and full-text papers - the former providing concise overviews and the latter offering in-depth analysis. We are interested in exploring how Q&A pairs from both text types can be utilized to enhance NLP models' understanding of document structure and the semantic complexity of professional communication.

In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a non-explosion from a 20 solar mass star. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, only the explosive model exhibited instability behind the shockwave due to the interaction between particles and neutrinos. This could be attributed to the level of angular velocity and mass distribution of the star. Our results show that in successful supernovae events, neutrino instability is less severe and has a smaller impact.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widely diagnosed psychiatric condition, yet there is still a need for objective biomarkers to facilitate its diagnosis. Researchers are using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) data in combination with machine learning algorithms in an attempt to find a more reliable diagnostic method. A deep learning algorithm known as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has been successfully applied to rs-fMRI data and achieves high accuracy in classifying ADHD patients by selectively discarding non-essential brain regions. This study aims to identify the critical components of the brain that are utilized by CNN through a process called network importance analysis. The outcomes show that CNN places a significant emphasis on regions involving the default mode network (DMN) as well as the cerebellum, specifically its anterior portion. When incorporating these essential regions into the diagnosis, CNN's accuracy improved from 71% to 76%, outperforming previous studies and confirming the significance of the cerebellum in ADHD diagnosis.

In a discrete-time network where disease propagation occurs randomly, the model considers two distinct categories of individuals: those who have contracted the disease and are infectious, and those who have not and are susceptible. Assuming infinite disease capacity and a discrete-time framework, we develop a model that represents an outbreak in a homogeneous network and derive an explicit expression for the outbreak size. Furthermore, we determine the conditions under which an outbreak occurs and establish that small initial infected nodes can trigger an outbreak. Our study and analysis provide insight into how an outbreak propagates within the network.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing styles and genres. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. As a result, identifying and resolving acronyms has emerged as a critical task across multiple fields, and an increasing number of researchers are turning to machine learning and data-driven approaches to tackle this challenge. To facilitate collaboration and experimentation, there is an ongoing need for user-friendly, integrated platforms that can be employed for teaching acronym identification and disambiguation, research, and application development. In response, we present MadDog, a comprehensive web-based tool that provides a dataset of acronym definitions, along with features for sentence encoding and decoding, as well as a range of evaluation metrics. To demonstrate the platform's capabilities, we also outline the development process of a deep learning-based model named DeepAbb, which outperforms alternative methods on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, MadDog offers a knowledge base of acronym definitions and supports related research and application development initiatives.

Quantum interference, evident in quantum interference effect, plays a significant role in the unique functioning of electronic devices in the quantum Hall regime. This includes electromagnetic waves interacting with charge carriers producing auto-resonant phenomena and enhanced thermoelectric currents that can switch on and off. Additionally, these interference effects can be utilized to efficiently direct heat in microelectronic devices, even over extended distances. This research extensively explores the relationship between quantum interference and heat rectification, revealing various underlying physical mechanisms. Furthermore, experiments based on samples with multiple paths such as loops, gratings, and interferometers have been conducted to observe these phenomena. Notably, electron thermoelectric current in response to temperature differences can be increased by up to 300 times through spatial heat rectification. This research may lead to significant advancements in microelectronic thermoelectric devices, potentially enabling increased energy conversion efficiency and device miniaturization.

The storage capacity of our world's data is rapidly growing, not only in size but also in volume, necessitating innovative solutions to manage information efficiently. Recently, researchers have explored the possibility of utilizing DNA technology for data storage due to its impressive capacity to store data biologically. Current approaches, however, suffer from several drawbacks, including complicated file structures, outdated data, and labor-intensive updating processes. To address these limitations, this paper presents an innovative hierarchical DNA storage framework that adapts the widely-used B-tree data structure to a DNA storage paradigm. By incorporating a unique combination of fixed and variable length DNA segments, this framework enhances file organization, retrieval efficiency, and data update speed while maintaining a constant physical storage capacity. Furthermore, our design is versatile and can be applied to various existing DNA access methods with adaptated parameters, demonstrating excellent performance in simulation studies.

Topological insulators are distinguished by robust edge states that safeguard their exceptional properties. A particular feature, topological degeneracy, is inherent in Weyl points and nodal lines, which are emerging as important entities in condensed matter physics. This introduction outlines the momentum-space analogues of nodal lines and highlights recent realizations in photonic, plasmonic, and other systems. It also addresses key challenges in replicating these idealized states within experimental systems and their inherent flaws.

In oscillatory media, regions that exhibit autonomous activity, like pacemaker points, can give rise to propagating wave patterns. These waves are triggered when a critical threshold of activated cells is reached, leading to a rapid increase in the wave's front. We have developed analytical methods to estimate the speed of these wave patterns. Our initial approach, applicable to highly nonuniform initial conditions, reveals that the wave's rapid development is largely influenced by the rate at which the pacemaker area expands. Conversely, when the initial conditions are closely aligned with the natural frequency of the medium, our second method provides a speed estimation that is largely independent of the pacemaker area's size. We have also conducted numerical simulations to validate our analytical findings, with specific examples drawn from columnar structures comprising excitatory core and inhibitory shell cells.

We have developed two quantum algorithms that determine the entropy of a quantum system within a specified error margin, using fewer operations than was previously thought possible. Given a quantum state |ψ〉 whose density matrix has eigenvalues λ_i, we can calculate the entropy H(ρ) = -∑λ_i log(λ_i) with the following levels of accuracy: for the weak case, we achieve ε precision at the cost of Õ(√n/ε^2) operations, and for the strong case, we achieve ε precision with Õ(n^0/ε) operations when the largest eigenvalue λ_max is less than λ_i for i ≤ λ_max/ε. These algorithms work well for estimating the entropy of states produced by quantum circuits, and we show that similar approaches are likely to be useful for other problems involving the matrix logarithm.

The implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) technology heavily depends on computational infrastructure, including data storage systems. This study examines the underlying technical aspects of storage systems that impact AI deployments, particularly to identify common issues. A comprehensive analysis is then conducted to identify resolution methods for these problems. By characterizing storage systems from multiple manufacturers, this research provides essential information for organizations planning AI projects, including understanding the implications of integrated storage systems on model execution and data processing workflows.

Electrocardiogram signals hold significant clinical value in the diagnosis and monitoring of heart disorders. However, manually labeling these signals with the relevant medical conditions based on 14 sections of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is an intricate, time-consuming task. To overcome this obstacle, we introduce a semi-self-supervised approach for automatically labeling the signals. By utilizing a neural network to generate incomplete ECG signal segments for the sections where the associated diseases are unknown, and then using a separate classifier to determine the relevant ICD codes, we train the system in two stages. During the initial training phase, we focus on sections with clear labels but unclassified signal segments, while the classifier for the subsequent phase is trained on all sections with unknown labels. When making predictions, our system combines the classifications from the two models. We tested this approach using the publicly available STAFF dataset, and compared it to three other advanced methods, yielding a macro-AUC of 0.922 for class 1 and 0.897 for class 2, outperforming the alternatives significantly.

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals, specifically those ideals for which one specific prime ideal $P$ among their prime divisors has a dimension equal to the codimension of the ideal. Such ideals have all prime divisors with dimensions not exceeding $1$ or all prime divisors with dimensions not exceeding one prime division away from the codimension. This class of ideals includes $x^4$-Stanley Depth 3 ideals and $x^5$-Stanley Depth 3 ideals. Nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals with specific depth properties in a given prime ideal also receive analysis.

Achieving efficient machine learning on large-scale quantum computers remains a major goal, particularly when working with complex, real-world data. Current text-based learning methods on superconducting devices face significant limitations due to real-time noise affecting their performance. Our study explores the potential of using quantum algorithms for unsupervised learning tasks, and we successfully demonstrate the first quantum-guided learning experiment on superconducting devices. By comparing the accuracy of quantum-based learning methods with classical approaches, we find that quantum algorithms perform similarly but require significantly fewer training samples. Our findings also show that a previously developed classical learning technique can be enhanced by incorporating quantum features, leading to improved classification results.

Our analysis encompasses all prime-field microlensing planets from the KMTNet AnomalyFinder algorithm in 2018, excluding those already reported in a previous study.  Out of 147 new planets, 125/147 (85%) were found to have been previously identified as planets by the KMTNet group through their official website or paper releases.  The primary method for a planet's identification as a microlensing event is by examining the debris motion on the microlensing plane, specifically looking for instances of planetary caustic tic or approximately circular Einstein radius patterns.  The code used to identify these planets is referred to as P4.  Each planet was manually reviewed by at least one author to verify its classification as a microlensing planet.  Additionally, our research calculates various planet characteristics and compares these to established microlensing planet population trends.

A new, accurate method for differentiable shadow rendering is introduced, allowing for improved performance in various computer vision applications. The 'ScreenSwap' model, based on a self-organizing map, enables efficient shadow detection and enhancement through an adaptable, high-resolution grid. The integration of a hierarchical depth estimation module facilitates precise 3D reconstruction of scenes containing complex geometries and multiple light sources. Evaluations confirm that the proposed approach surpasses state-of-the-art shadow rendering techniques and accelerates inverse lighting and 3D rendering tasks by 2x and 3x, respectively.

Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the importance of probabilistic models that account for uncertain demand and supply factors such as road conditions and traffic signals. Real-world data collection has become easier and more cost-effective due to the widespread use of smart cards and other technologies, generating substantial amounts of demand data. This paper develops an innovative framework to estimate an origin-destination demand matrix and associated variance matrix by maximizing a likelihood function and incorporating day-to-day network equilibrium equations. The proposed method determines the expected matrix and variance matrix through an iterative process alternating between ordinary least squares estimation and variance estimation. The approach is demonstrated using synthetic data and real-demand data from Croydon, UK.

In an array of oscillators with asymmetrical interactions and random frequencies, an in-depth analysis of synchronization patterns is conducted as frequencies gradually overlap and diverse connections between oscillators vary in strength. The study discovers multiple stages in synchronization: initially, local clusters form and synchronize within isolated components, then bridge connections facilitate the exchange of information and trigger a global synchronization transition. The observation period is focused on the dynamics preceding a prospective early onset of synchronization brought about by internal instability in the system. A detailed model includes heterogeneous oscillator elements with unidirectional asymmetrical connections, and by systematically adjusting connection strengths and oscillators' random frequencies, the system's behavior is extensively explored. The analysis provides precise thresholds for synchronization transitions in systems with specific topological structures and reveals distinct patterns of collective behavior in different states.

The Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms are well-known methods for generating random spanning trees within connected graphs. By adapting these algorithms to the presence of edge weights, a weighted spanning tree generation process can be achieved. Interestingly, the first-stage of Aldous-Broder's algorithm is equivalent to Wilson's loop erase algorithm when stopping at a random tree, and this equivalence leads to a faster and more practical implementation of Wilson's algorithm.

While significant progress has been made in learning joint representations from text and speech, music notation and audio present distinct challenges: they are inherently multi-modal and involve handling unstructured, symbol-based data. To overcome these obstacles, we developed MusicTM, a comprehensive dataset featuring a diverse collection of songs alongside both text-based and audio representations of lyrics and instrumentals. The music notation data, extracted from the Music21 library, includes both simplified and detailed versions, enabling us to investigate the impact of visual complexity on representation learning. With its 16,768 entries, MusicTM surpasses existing datasets, offering opportunities for extensive research and outperforming current baselines with its advanced multi-modal representation learning capabilities.

One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in its underwhelming user experience. To improve interaction, researchers have integrated Word2Vec embeddings into Ontodia diagrams to display human-friendly labels for entities in Wikidata. By utilizing these embeddings, Ontodia can generate more intuitive and descriptive labels for entities, enhancing the understanding of Linked Data for human users. This innovation has successfully been applied in various Ontodia-based applications, as demonstrated by a joint paper with David Vogel at the Semantic Application Challenge 2018.

We investigate the stability of dark solitons in optical systems with specific properties. These systems exhibit unique behavior due to non-linearity and varying dispersion properties, which can be influenced significantly by intensity-dependent dispersion. In our study, we focus on two types of dark solitons - those occurring in systems with cubic power-law non-linearity and those displaying a saturable dispersion characteristic. Our findings indicate that in systems with cubic power-law non-linearity, a specific arrangement of coefficients can lead to soliton stability at the core, surrounded by unstable radiation patterns. Conversely, for systems exhibiting a saturable dispersion characteristic, we observe that increased background intensity can result in stable dark soliton states. Our analytical results are supported by numerical simulations, which accurately reproduce our theoretical predictions and provide further insight into the behavior of dark solitons in optical systems with varying dispersion properties.

When users navigate a dataset, they frequently get lost in the analytical process, 
making it challenging to gain meaningful insights. Interactive visualizations and 
collaborative workflows can quickly lead to cognitive overload and misdirection.
To address this issue, experts have proposed various guidance methods within 
visual analytics. Unfortunately, the current infrastructure makes it difficult for 
researchers to share their knowledge effectively. To bridge this gap, we introduce 
Lotse: a flexible framework for implementing guidance methods. By providing a clear 
guideline and essential functionality, Lotse enables rapid development and 
evaluation of guidance methods. We demonstrate its efficacy by creating six diverse 
guidance methods using Lotse and successfully applying them in existing software 
systems. Through this approach, we aim to stimulate research and make guidance 
approaches more accessible and actionable.

A research framework focused on developing enhanced stellarators using enhanced coil positions has been developed, which can be applied to various configuration restoration methods. Preliminary results from the framework have yielded a substantial gain of approximately 30% in efficiency when applied to the NCSX design, which has also allowed for the integration of order-reducing coils within the framework's capabilities. These gains have been achieved without utilizing any explicit coil optimization processes.

A novel technique utilizing magnetic resonance thermometry and imaging has been implemented to determine temperature distributions within a gas-solid fixed bed under diverse conditions. The proposed method leverages the inherent spin resonance properties of gases to accurately measure temperatures as low as 73 Kelvin. The system's reliability has been validated through repeated temperature readings and assessments of temperature uniformity. Furthermore, temperature distributions have been successfully obtained using rapid two-dimensional imaging, and the proposed system has shown the ability to operate at gas flow rates typical of industrial-scale fixed beds.

In cellular environments, numerous large molecular complexes assemble from various proteins to execute vital functions, requiring precise regulation through aggregation control to ensure proper operation. To address this, researchers have developed a mathematical framework for understanding the aggregation of molecules that share components, based on a lattice-based model, to investigate how shared molecules affect aggregation. The model allows for the analysis of early stages of aggregation using mathematical techniques and numerical methods. The results show that when all molecules are available for interaction, the aggregation pattern follows a symmetrical pattern, with characteristics independent of the size of the aggregates. However, when molecules are limited, smaller aggregates form preferentially, and larger aggregates are formed by combining existing aggregates, rather than new ones. The latter process exhibits size-dependent aggregation patterns. The research provides insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the formation of shared biomolecular complexes.

Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major sunspot rotated in NOAA AR 11429 from September 16-18, 2012. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, influenced by strong magnetic disturbances including a major disruption and fragmentation that caused the sunspot to break into smaller areas. Analyzing the rotation of sunspots, we found that those that rotated in unconventional directions were located in areas of the sunspot where significant magnetic disturbances occurred, including areas where the sunspot fragmented. These results suggest that strong magnetic disturbances can cause sunspots to rotate in unconventional directions, especially in areas where the sunspots fragment.

We utilize the b-principle in an approach to prove topological invariance of Floer homology across a wide range of symplectic manifolds. This methodology also enables us to derive multiple corollaries alongside the Maudin conjecture.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of advanced multilevel preconditioning techniques for cardiac simulation systems, focusing on flexible, expandable configurations that can be applied to a range of models without significant modifications. A thorough examination is conducted of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for finite element discretizations on unstructured meshes, with an emphasis on the effect of subdomain decomposition, coarse space construction, and interpolation strategy. Computational experiments are performed using a standard finite element model of the heart and lungs, both with and without a novel adaptive coarse space method. Results indicate that the performance of these techniques significantly depends on the quality of the subdomain decomposition; however, the experimental implementation does not support automated domain splitting. Therefore, users need to manually specify the domain partitioning to optimize the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints method for distinct problem configurations.

The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is fundamentally transforming the digital landscape. Systems involving user-based content creation, such as tags, are now standard in various applications and have become essential for content description, search engine optimization, and data analysis. Due to their rapid adoption and widespread use, understanding the behavior and patterns of users within tag-based systems has become a pressing research need. This study aims to identify common patterns in user behavior within tag-based systems by analyzing existing datasets and establishing key characteristics of these systems. The research reveals key metrics that can help in designing and evaluating the effectiveness of tag-based systems and suggests areas where further research is required to gain deeper insights into user interactions within these systems.

A pioneering technique in mold insertion metagratings utilizes traditional photolithography to fabricate microscopic structures that control light propagation at the boundary between two mediums. However, this technique faces challenges at ultra-high frequencies such as photoresist post-processing and limited resolution, restricting operation to lower frequency ranges. A possible remedy is presented by a novel approach using two-photon photopolymerization to manufacture high-resolution microstructures in a photopolymer medium directly usable in mold insertion metagratings up to 300 GHz frequencies.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE ribbon model. Under the condition that the initial energy is relatively low, we demonstrate that the solutions are durable over any period of time. Furthermore, as time progresses indefinitely, the solutions converge to equilibrium in a unified manner.

Implementing Internet Architecture-Based approach inside mobile devices poses significant difficulties due to inherent mobile network problems and insufficient device resources. This implementation requires mobile devices to have a reliable host ID system and efficient packet processing capabilities, as well as sufficient resources to support ongoing connections. The emergence of Mobile Internet of Things (IoT) has created additional complexities in implementing the new architecture, driven by issues like connection multiplicity, persistent connection requirements, and resource constraints. This paper introduces the fundamental problems and proposed solutions associated with implementing the internet architecture-based approach in mobile devices. Furthermore, it discusses the key challenges involved and presents potential future research directions.

When tackling complex optimization challenges, researchers often turn to evolutionary algorithms, but their original design assumes certain conditions are met. In reality, real-world problems frequently deviate from these assumptions, necessitating the use of hyperparameters to modify the algorithms' behavior. Despite this, the process of selecting suitable hyperparameters is typically overlooked, with the understanding that some choices may yield better results, but without clear evidence. This study aims to shed light on the impact of hyperparameters on the effectiveness of these algorithms, employing three global sensitivity analysis methods to examine their ranking and influence. By utilizing a large dataset of benchmark functions, including the WARS collection, which simulates real-world scenarios with varying nonlinear constraints, this study evaluates the sensitivity of six evolutionary algorithm-based approaches. The findings suggest that some hyperparameters have a significant impact on effectiveness, while others have a minimal influence, and the ranking of significant hyperparameters differs depending on the chosen method. This study also highlights the importance of further research into the relationship between hyperparameter values and algorithm performance.

The paper presents an argument for adopting the wave formula as the fundamental building block of quantum theory. This is achieved by interpreting measurements as comparative judgments made by observers. Initially, the wave function is interpreted as a tool for predicting measurement results, but subsequent interpretations consider the wave function itself to be a direct expression of physical reality and objective comparison standards, respectively. When the first interpretation is based on a classical likelihood ratio and the second interpretation is grounded in a von Mises-style objective frequency concept, two equivalent versions of the Born rule emerge, thereby providing an intrinsic justifications for this quantification principle commonly employed in quantum theory. This justification also addresses a long-standing concern about the Born rule being merely a empirical convention. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the wave formula remains applicable even in complex scenarios involving multiple entangled systems separated by large distances.

Despite significant advancements in reinforcement learning, creating AI agents that can consistently perform well in the long term remains a complex challenge. Developing reinforcement learning methods that can adapt to changing environments over an agent's entire lifespan is a key area of research. To accelerate the pace of innovation in this field, there is a need for a comprehensive simulation framework that can simulate an agent's entire lifespan. This paper presents L2Explorer, a groundbreaking tool that enables the evaluation of reinforcement learning methods across an extensive range of dynamic environments. By leveraging L2Explorer, researchers can test and assess the lifelong performance of reinforcement learning algorithms. Based on an in-depth analysis of L2Explorer, our results demonstrate that a straightforward reinforcement learning approach can achieve remarkable outcomes, particularly when the environment is relatively stable. However, when the environment is highly unpredictable and constantly evolving, even this approach underperforms in comparison to state-of-the-art methods.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with Adaptive Optics Systems like Naidu or WISPY, and deliver a combined field of view of about 100 x 150 inches or 8.3 x 12.7 arcseconds. Liger's data stream will be extremely high-rate, over 20 gigabits per second, necessitating substantial preprocessing within its control system to compress the data into 2-3 gigabits per second for transmission to the central master computer. This processing system will employ a range of specialized hardware and software components, and we outline the design and implementation details of its data processing system, as well as the interfaces for data transmission and manipulation.

This study uncovers a broad class of smooth, time-dependent solutions in 2D Euler's equation that deviate only slightly from Couette flow, spanning all intermediate speeds between viscous and inviscid limits. These solutions involve coupling a shear layer with a counter-rotating vortex streak to produce traveling waves, with the vortex streak's intensity capable of being adjusted to fit either the Reynolds number beta-plane or the beta-spectrum models commonly observed in geostrophic turbulence.

We experimentally investigate how optical pulses affect linear polarization in gonian spinor exciton-polariton condensates by modifying the cavity's linear polarization using rotating quarter-wave plates. Varying the pulse intensity, orientation, and duration allows us to control the final polarization state of the cavity, achieving either a pure linear or hybrid polarization, depending on the circumstances. Our results are further supported by numerical simulations, which reveal how excitation and coherent interaction influence polarization evolution.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations including non-local slope terms. The specific focus lies within a particular class of nonlocal equations formulated within the context of a stochastic framework on a one-dimensional domain. The main drive behind these nonlocal equations is to understand how they interact with already established local Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equations. The main outcome of this work is a sharp condition that ensures solutions to these nonlocal equations will eventually deviate from solutions to their corresponding local counterparts.

The COVID-19 pandemic triggered significant data sharing initiatives, making vast amounts of data accessible to the public under permissive licenses. This research analyzed freely available COVID-19 data from various sources, including public health platforms and individual dashboards, to illustrate their impact on policy decisions in South Africa. A comparative analysis of eight key indicators revealed that multiple datasets consistently tracked the pandemic's progression in different provinces. Furthermore, the study demonstrated how machine learning techniques could be used to identify the most reliable datasets based on correlation coefficients. In exploring the geographic distribution of deaths, the study found that South African datasets lack disaggregated spatial information, highlighting a critical need for spatial analytics in COVID-19 research. This study contributes to the literature by showcasing the effectiveness of collaborative data collection and highlights potential applications of machine learning in understanding the pandemic through publicly accessible data.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem posits the following: given sets A and B, each with n elements, if the sum of their intersection's cardinality is less than n, then there exists a subset of A with 2n elements such that its difference with respect to set B is a subset of {0, d, 2d}. This paper asserts the validity of a stronger statement: given sets A and B, each with n elements, if the sum of their intersection's cardinality is less than n, then a subset of A with 2n elements exists along with a subgroup G of the integers such that the following conditions are met: the difference of set A with respect to set B is a subset of {0, g}, and the group G contains an element other than 0.

In medical fields, large datasets are frequently encountered, where doctors need to analyze a large amount of information to make informed decisions. Recent advancements in multiple imaging technologies and sophisticated computer technologies now enable rapid and precise data collection, helping medical professionals to assess diseases more effectively. Our research applies various computer vision techniques to optic disc analysis, retinal fundus images, and optical coherence tomography images, then integrates the results with other relevant data to create a comprehensive understanding of diseases. By leveraging these technologies, we have developed classifiers for glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy that are highly accurate and adaptable to different datasets.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to overwhelming cases of patients with life-threatening respiratory conditions, stripping hospitals of resources and forcing them to make desperate life-or-death decisions about admissions. To effectively allocate healthcare resources, there's an urgent need for a rapid and efficient diagnostic system that can identify patients' treatment priority during emergency ICU admissions. Research has demonstrated that deep learning models can quickly analyze medical images to extract patients' critical information. We've discovered that certain patterns in chest X-ray images, such as lung density, can indicate the severity of COVID-19 and potentially the patient's health condition. Building on this knowledge, we've developed an image analysis model that integrates both respiratory and cardiovascular aspects to identify patients' critical information. We've also confirmed that the proposed model outperforms existing solutions through comprehensive testing.

This research focuses on recovering the boundary characteristics of an acoustic scattering medium through transmission eigenfunctions, which are theoretically and numerically investigated in a two-dimensional setting involving spherical media. Transmission eigenfunctions are generated under a media boundary interface, and theoretical and numerical tools are developed to reconstruct this interface from measured far-field patterns of the scattered wave. To facilitate this process, a special transform is introduced, enabling the boundary shape to be resolved through a related integral equation involving the transformed scattering wave. Our findings are then validated through a series of numerical experiments.

To effectively utilize a dialogue system for an unknown task, it must first comprehend the user's intent, even if the dialogue history and target intent class have never been encountered before during training. This research proposes a novel intent discovery approach, comprising pre-training with unfolding conversation simulations and a novel contrastive learning framework. Initially, the method leverages a pre-trained language model to derive intent-related information from entire conversations. Then, a custom-designed network structure enables the model to distinguish between intent classes based on contextualized dialogue representations. Furthermore, the PCDL framework dynamically matches dialogues from the history to the query, enhancing the model's ability to generalize across unseen histories and intent classes. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over state-of-the-art approaches in intent discovery, with notable generalization improvements when applied to intent classification.

The R. Brown - P. Steed universal simplicial group construction has received attention for its potential applications, including a detailed examination by G. Malgoud in the context of nonabelian tensor categories. Following R. Brown and G. Malgoud's work, we demonstrate that the universal simplicial collection \mathcal{U} constructs a simplicial group when a unit is defined that satisfies certain conditions. Notably, these conditions are met by the bilinear map describing the tensor product of two comonoidal functors. As a result, we show that the functor mapping a functorial simplicial set \mathcal{F} to the group \mathcal{U}\mathcal{F} is a homotopy equivalence for any functorial simplicial group G.

In our analysis, we establish that the total count of subgroups belonging to various types (isomorphic to a given finite group $G$ and falling within a specific type) is limited by $2^{d+o(1)}$, where $d$ represents the depth of the permutation action underlying the subgroup type. Moreover, we prove that the exponent can be replaced by $2^{o(1)}$ when $d$ is sufficiently large. Our findings are sustained by the recent results of Larsen and Tiep for type 2 groups and the work of Breuillard, Garami, and Tillich on the growth of subgroups in soluble groups. To our knowledge, this study provides the first explicit upper bound on the count of subgroups of a given type that can occur within a finite group of permutation length $d$.

This paper examines in detail the Au Belashov Bogaevskii H2 equation, a significant model used in the study of quasilinear scalar partial differential equations. We discuss the equation's general solution, obtained through the fusion of two compatible simple partial differential equations. The text also explores connections between the H2 equation and other notable equations in the field, particularly the Camassa Holm equation.

This paper tackles the visual relationship detection task, a challenging one in computer vision due to false positives stemming from irrelevant proposals that aren't addressed by existing methods. We've developed an end-to-end ranking model that identifies and minimizes these false positives by the relationship type and proposal content. Our model, called ConRerank, incorporates a dynamic weighting system for proposals according to their likelihood of containing the targeted objects, as well as a false positive rejection strategy that adapts to the complexity of relationships on a case-by-case basis. We've extensively evaluated ConRerank on the VRD dataset and found it to substantially outperform leading methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score across various relationship types, with some improvements exceeding 10%.

A new price theorem relates the postweak measurement quantum correlation to the premeasurement quantum correlation, revealing that noncommuting operators generate both types of correlation. This reveals a crucial property of quantum systems, where the postweak measurement correlation is not only influenced by the measurement process but also by the premeasurement state, as evidenced by the quantum correlation price (QCP). This price can be utilized to calculate the postweak measurement correlation for any state given a specific Hamiltonian and pair of noncommuting operators. The study also demonstrates that the QCP depends on both the premeasurement state and the measurement strength. Consequently, the QCP can be viewed as a measure of quantum influence arising from system-premeasurement interaction. The research further illustrates that the QCP is bounded by a specific value (the maximum quantum correlation price (MQCP)), which can be reached for specific pure states but remains unreachable for mixed states due to their inherent mixed nature.

Artificial intelligence's interest in social networks is piqued due to their potential in training relationship-aware models. Nevertheless, generating large-scale networks with accurate connections and varied relationships for training such models is a daunting task. While human-generated data like Kinship and Family can serve this purpose, its limitations in diversity and scalability become apparent when trying to model complex social relationships. This paper introduces an neural network-based approach that can create synthetic social networks with specified characteristics, making it more practical and efficient than manually created networks when it comes to training relationship-aware models.

To effectively capture and propagate visual information and dependencies among remote peers during vision tasks, we propose a communication method called Dynamic Graph Communication Passing Networks. This approach redefines communication within deep networks by representing the connection between nodes as a dynamic graph that undergoes changes at each data processing stage. This innovation enables each node to maintain a global spatial structure, allowing them to selectively aggregate and pass information to other nodes. Furthermore, we introduce a novel aggregation mechanism that enables nodes to transmit distinct information to the receiving node, leading to more efficient information transmission. This mechanism's superiority over traditional methods is demonstrated through experimental results showing enhanced performance of the DCPN architecture on various vision benchmarks, resulting in a significant improvement of 2.07% over the baseline model for semantic segmentation and 4.41% for image classification.

Optimized hardware is crucial when executing efficient signal processing tasks after an inside-out approximation of a modular arithmetic reconfiguration, like that found in the SLAC unit. One cost optimization technique specifically targets MCMP tasks, seeking to eliminate unnecessary multipliers from reconfigured architectures. Although previous works have addressed this issue, they fail to provide a thorough analysis or a reliable solution when dealing with large multipliers or a vast number of constants. This paper presents a novel approach to resolve this optimization problem, offering a precise guantity of solution quality and thorough comparative studies. The proposed method has been successfully validated through both silicon and software proofs.

Recent breakthroughs in quantum computing have opened doors for potential advancements in machine learning, particularly with the increasing development of hybrid quantum neural networks. These hybrid models, combining quantum and classical elements, offer promising avenues for addressing the significant shortcomings of large neural networks. This paper delves into the core concepts behind quantum neural networks, discusses the progress made so far, and explores the challenges and uncertainties surrounding this emerging field. Furthermore, it provides insights into potential future directions and highlights pivotal research studies in this area.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator community is driven by a relentless pursuit to
minimize energy consumption, weight and heat generation from its systems.  Over the
past four years, significant breakthroughs have been achieved in innovative RF
technologies, such as compact RF guns, deflection and bending cavities, fast-switching
amplifiers and new gap technologies.  This report outlines recommendations for
research priorities to future particle physics programs, detailing technical advances
and proposing fresh avenues for investigation to advance particle physics and related
fields.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

We have extended previously established relations for linearized waves in perfect fluids to models with viscosity and heat transfer. By building on the second law of irreversible thermodynamics, we have formulated a conserved current with the correct divergence, leading to a definition of relativistic entropy gradient. This formulation takes into account the diversity of irreversible thermodynamic theories that can be applied to fluid dynamics. We have shown that when the fluid's viscous effects become negligible, our model converges to the established Einstein's equations and the wave relations for non-viscous fluids. Additionally, we have derived specific wave relations for fluids with specific types of viscosity and heat transfer.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of gamma-rays and neutrinos could be used to determine the mass of primordial black holes (PBHs) that might have formed early in the universe, providing insights into models that propose PBHs as a potential source of dark matter. These PBHs would have formed when matter overdensities developed early in the universe, supernova explosions expanded and eventually collapsed, or when cosmic strings broke and formed early universes. Initially, the temperature of these PBHs would have been equal to the universe's temperature, causing them to emit Hawking radiation and eventually resulting in a cosmic background of gamma-rays and neutrinos that can be observed. By analyzing this background, we can determine the mass of PBHs and therefore assess the universes in which they formed. Our study shows that PBHs formed early in the universe would have masses in the range of milligrams to metric tons and would have temperatures ranging from microKelvin to trillion degrees Kelvin. Additionally, our research confirms that the cosmic background of neutrinos and gamma-rays would have temperatures and densities below the universe's temperature and density, approximately equivalent to a redshift of 3,000.

This research introduces the Virtual Safeguard Platform, a modular tool that integrates the Safeguard Processor with communications systems, across multiple hardware platforms. To facilitate efficient system implementation, we develop a programmable platform, the Virtual Safeguard Platform, comprising a programmable communication component and programmable memory cells. Our approach is to implement the ISP within the Unitaon-Matunb-Safrud-Din (UMSD) protocol, leveraging the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) provided by Intel SGX or hardware-based PCHMC on AMD FHE-based systems. To optimize performance, we devise five-stage pipeline processors: the FHE-accumulator (VFP) and FHE-comparator (VFC), both over FHE. To enhance security, we incorporate an optional step for FHE-verification (VF) and FHE-rewrapping (WR) within the pipeline. Our novel five-stage pipeline processor design caters to various security needs, offering a versatile tool for developers to utilize in safeguarding applications. Through performance evaluation, we show that our safeguarded processor achieves satisfactory speeds, 1.65 million KE/WS, while maintaining an exceptionally low L1E/WS rate of 0.0003.

We develop a convex general-valued optimization algorithm applicable to a broad range of problems, including those with sparse constraints and objectives. Our approach yields pseudo-algorithms with approximate solutions even in the most challenging scenarios of (strongly) polynomial time and poly-hierarchy levels. We achieve this by combining sequential re-scaling techniques with the polyhedral decomposition method, thereby significantly expanding the class of problems amenable to such solutions. Our work significantly enhances previous research and facilitates the derivation of PTAS for intricate optimization problems with vast applications.

Recent breakthroughs in NLP have been fueled by the widespread adoption of large pre-trained language models like RoBERTa and Elephants. These models, once trained on a task, can perform it exceptionally well even on unseen data, providing valuable insights into their capabilities. This study investigates whether these models can analyze text without explicit labels by employing a range of unsupervised and few-shot evaluations across multiple NLP tasks and data sets. The results show that while they perform admirably in many scenarios, enhancing task-specific knowledge through labeled data significantly improves performance. Moreover, incorporating task-specific fine-tuning yields substantial gains, but this process necessitates access to labeled data, contradicting the initial query. Notably, the few-shot evaluation reveals that leveraging the model's top-k analyzed samples during fine-tuning can isolate task-relevant information and facilitate efficient learning from limited labeled data.

High-definition hyperspectral images contain numerous spectral layers, which could potentially serve as a refined and structured source for pixel-level semantic information. Nevertheless, directly converting these spectral layers into meaningful visual categories proves to be an intricate task. In this research, we develop an advanced and resource-efficient approach for semantic segmentation by leveraging hyperspectral images, which requires minimal domain-specific knowledge. Initially, we utilize a self-organizing neural network called the hyperspectral image transformer to extract relevant semantic features from the hyperspectral image. Subsequently, we employ a downstream classifier for refining the extracted features and adapting them to the specific requirements of the target semantic task. To minimize data constraints, we also incorporate an unsupervised data augmentation technique called the spectral shift, which swaps spectral layers between images to broaden the model's data exposure. Moreover, we introduce a supervised learning stage to fine-tune the model, utilizing labeled datasets whenever available. Our proposed approach demonstrates superior performance on the Cityscape dataset, especially under hyperspectral image conditions, which often mimics various real-world imaging scenarios.

The evolution of solar-type stars is closely tied to their internal rotation velocity, which can be measured from surface characteristics like magnetic field patterns or sunspots. These measurements indicate that some solar-type stars have high rotation velocities, which can't be explained by conventional internal rotation models that rely on core convection and differential rotation. We've found that these high-rotation velocities can be attributed to either the star's core consuming lighter elements or another unknown process that redistributes angular momentum. If we attribute the high-rotation velocities to core consumption, it suggests that lighter elements are consumed at a rate that's higher than expected, leading to a star that's too small. Alternatively, if we're looking at the early stages of solar-type star development, it could indicate that there's another process that redistributes angular momentum, which isn't yet well understood.

In this study, we examine the computational model of random access machines with the ability to perform basic addition operations and derive a lower bound on the time required for specific operations like multiplication, division, and modulus operations within this framework. Specifically, our research shows that while modulus operations can be carried out in $O(\log n)$ time by utilizing only addition, the same cannot be said for division, which necessitates at least $O(n)$ time. We establish a connection between these results and a well-known concept in number theory, demonstrating that if we can efficiently (linear time complexity) perform division, it implies a similar capability for factoring numbers, thereby violating a certain hypothesis if it holds true. Additionally, our research involves analyzing the circuit complexity of these operations, thereby extending existing lower bound results for specific operations like division and modulus in circuit models to random access machine models with addition.

To address the issue of providing personalized recommendations to users based on search history, we develop a Session-oriented Recommendation (SOR) framework. This approach leverages user browsing patterns in e-commerce to build detailed user profiles and enhances existing session-based recommendation methods by incorporating graph neural networks. However, current SOR models face two major limitations. Firstly, they rely heavily on labeled data, a scarce resource in real-world scenarios. Secondly, they fail to take full advantage of the rich information available within both the session and graph domains. To overcome these challenges, we propose an unsupervised graph co-training framework, where two identical models are trained in an alternating manner using self-supervised session and graph branches. This approach enables the SOR model to exploit information from both domains without the constraints of labeled data. We evaluate our method by conducting extensive experiments on real-world datasets and comparing it against state-of-the-art baseline models.

This research presents two types of codes: Group LCD codes and Group Reversible LCM codes. The articles initial part introduces necessary concepts and establishes a link between Group LCD codes and Reversible LCM codes. Building on this foundation, the article develops a method to create Group LCD codes using the transversal embedding technique. Utilizing a method from [20], a larger code can be formed from a smaller Group LCD code, allowing for varying rates of the resulting code. Separate examples illustrate the construction of high-rate Group LCD codes and high-rate Reversible LCM codes.

A new theory is developed combining differential forms with combinatorial face areas to assign a meaningful concept of volume to the geometric shapes formed by simplicial complexes. This theoretical framework is applied to calculate Feynman integrals, and it is demonstrated that Stokes theorem regulates observable quantities such as numerators of scattering processes and their infinite volumes, also known as scale-invariant parts. The approach is initially explored using tree-level examples, and then it is extended to consider loop corrections.

In a recent study, a recurrent neural network's performance in an object categorization task was examined after being trained using commonly occurring object shapes. It was discovered that the network's internal state or hidden variables consistently reflected characteristics of the visual input stimuli such as size, orientation, and binocularity. Additionally, it was found that the network's hidden variables remained stable across different images containing objects from the same category, but varying images within a single category showed high variability in the network's internal state. Furthermore, the network's performance was better when presented with images containing category-consistent object traits as opposed to those with inconsistent traits. This effect was more pronounced for complex 3D object categories than for simpler shapes.

In one-dimensional systems with Hermitian Hamiltonians, point-node topological features occur when the spectrum intersects zero at isolated points, leading to anomalous edge states that cannot be localized physically. We demonstrate that in non-Hermitian systems, correlations between fermions reduce the number of isolated point nodes in the spectrum from three to one, with the intermediate node disappearing entirely. This outcome is confirmed through calculations using both bosonization and exact models, with additional findings indicating that correlations introduce a continuous range in the spectrum and transfer point nodes between different momentum segments.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained significant interest due to their utility in Golay complementary matrices-based spatial modulation systems. This innovative modulation technique offers several superior characteristics such as simplified detection processes and enhanced data transfer rates. While various Golay complementary matrix designs are already available, the existing spectra of these matrices are often non-uniform, which can hinder the efficiency of spatial modulation systems. To address this issue, this research proposes a multi-dimensional Golay complementary matrix design that ensures synchronized time and frequency domains. We demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing these matrices in CM arrays through feasible unitary CM constructions. Notably, our designs yield identical magnitude spectra, facilitating more adaptable and efficient spatial modulation systems.

Research on Higgs boson production is conducted in a final state with four charged leptons using 12.4/fb of LHC data at 13 TeV. The investigation includes both on-shell and off-shell Higgs boson cases to broaden understanding. By comparing measured outcomes with theoretical predictions of different scenarios, limitations on the Higgs boson width and anomalous interactions are determined. The analysis reveals constraints on the Higgs boson width ranging from 0.4 to 5.4 MeV, and restrictions on anomalous HVV couplings are also established, including coupling variations up to 7 TeV in the absence of a signal or up to 0.7 TeV in the presence of a signal.

Hyperspectral image analysis plays a vital role in remote sensing and industrial applications, and change detection is a valuable aspect for understanding and interpreting these images. This process is essential for identifying and acknowledging changes within hyperspectral images, and thus, various techniques have been developed for effective change detection. This study introduces an unsupervised change detection method for hyperspectral images using a novel approach based on deep convolutional neuromodulators. Utilizing a dual-network structure, this method combines the unique capabilities of convolutional neural networks and the binary neuromodular to efficiently extract and utilize sparse features from hyperspectral images. This leads to an accurate and data-driven change detection result, and our experiments conduct extensive evaluations on real-world datasets to demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method.

This paper explores the outcomes of combining elements from two distinct sets, each of which consists solely of squares, in the context of additive problems within the realm of non-zero integers. Building upon past research by Erdos and Pomerance, we demonstrate the existence of infinitely many natural numbers, twin primes, and prime powers that cannot be expressed as the sum of two perfect squares. Additionally, we address a particular inquiry raised by Erdos in a broader context and offer insights into the feasibility of achieving specific upper limits for the expressed sums.

Quantum bits in silicon don't lose information easily, making them ideal for large-scale quantum computing. A recent study has demonstrated the simultaneous occurrence of two key processes in silicon: valence state shifting and spin spin-flipping within a single atom at the atomic level. This was achieved by creating and manipulating a specific combination of orbitals called a $\Delta$ valley state, thereby causing neighboring silicon atoms to flip their electron spins. Utilizing a sophisticated simulation technique known as ab-initio density matrix purification, the researchers were able to model and analyze this phenomenon in silicon crystals. This breakthrough has significant implications for the development of quantum bits in silicon, allowing for the rapid manipulation of atoms within the crystal structure through the use of light or magnetic fields, thereby enhancing the performance of quantum computing circuits.

In various computational optimization challenges, solution methods like Evolutionary Algorithms, have proven valuable and have been extensively studied through both theoretical and experimental means. Following in the footsteps of other successful open-source software initiatives such as Pulse and Ray, we introduce LibOPT - an open-source framework aimed at facilitating research into novel nature-inspired optimization techniques. By providing a comprehensive set of tools, including a graphical user interface for data analysis and a benchmark suite of problems with easily accessible code, LibOPT supports the rapid development and empirical evaluation of new algorithms. Featuring multi-objective optimization support and a wide range of algorithmic components, such as permutation matrices generation and Tchebycheff-based data normalization, LibOPT is an extensive resource for researchers and developers of optimization algorithms.

This study focuses on specific algebraic systems where every element has the same size in terms of the algebra's structure. We investigate shapes defined by irreducible factors with repeated symptoms, establishing equivalent criteria based on transitivity and degree. This work also examines how shapes related to transitivity can be described using symmetric groups, infinite solvable length, and nilpotent groups of a specific rank.

In non-commutative spacetimes, the identity of particles becomes ambiguous due to the non-commutativity of field components. This issue arises when field operators with different indices do not commute, causing mixed field solutions to represent multiple particle states. We examine the problem of quantum fields in non-commutative spacetimes, particularly with non-commutativity of position-space components, where the issue is particularly evident. Matrices representing the identity operator lose their distinctive identity when transformed into momentum-space, highlighting the non-unique nature of particle identification. We investigate the implications of this issue on single-particle states and demonstrate that multiple states correspond to the same single-particle state, with interactions inducing particle number changes. The nature of scattering processes is examined, along with the concept of particle conservation, which may need revision or reinterpretation.

We introduce an advanced technique called TWAT, which combines transient voltage and two-photon absorption to study 3D charge transport in wide bandgap semiconductors, particularly demonstrating its effectiveness in CVD diamond. This is achieved by correlating the optical excitation density of nitrogen-vacancy centers with measured ionic charge. TWAT leverages the unique properties of the NV center to simultaneously serve as both an optical excitation marker and a shallow trap capturing ionic charge. This is enabled through a custom-designed sample holder for optical and electrical connections. As demonstrated, TWAT enables the mapping of 3D charge transport, identification of trap states, and an in-depth analysis of the bulk and surface properties of diamond. This approach also presents opportunities for applying TWAT in other NV-based materials and systems.
